author: Pliny the Elder
provenance: LacusCurtius (Mayhoff/Teubner edition) — NOT the Latin Library; this book is absent from the Latin Library corpus and was fetched separately, normalized to the corpus's plain-text style.

pairs.source_text: produntur Arimaspi, quos diximus, uno oculo in fronte media insignes. quibus adsidue bellum esse circa metalla cum grypis, ferarum volucri genere, quale vulgo traditur, eruente ex cuniculis aurum, mira cupiditate et feris custodientibus et Arimaspis rapientibus, multi, sed maxime inlustres Herodotus et Aristeas Proconnesius scribunt.
pairs.question: Quo corporis insigni Arimaspos notari Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: By what bodily peculiarity does Pliny say the Arimaspi are marked?
pairs.answer_en: By a single eye in the middle of the forehead.
pairs.derivation: The one-eyed Arimaspi of the far north, a fixture of ancient ethnography from Herodotus and Aristeas onward. Anchored to the named people; the answer is stated verbatim (uno oculo in fronte media insignes). Closed-book and part of the shared stock of ancient world-geography.

pairs.source_text: quibus adsidue bellum esse circa metalla cum grypis, ferarum volucri genere, quale vulgo traditur, eruente ex cuniculis aurum, mira cupiditate et feris custodientibus et Arimaspis rapientibus, multi, sed maxime inlustres Herodotus et Aristeas Proconnesius scribunt.
pairs.question: Cum quo genere ferarum Arimaspos circa aurum adsidue bellare traditur?
pairs.question_en: With what kind of beasts are the Arimaspi said to wage continual war over gold?
pairs.derivation: The perpetual war of the Arimaspi with the gold-guarding griffins. Anchored to the named people; single answer (grypes) supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the best-known marvels of the ancient north, cited by Pliny from Herodotus and Aristeas.

pairs.source_text: similis et in Africa Psyllorum gens fuit, ut Agatharchides scribit, a Psyllo rege dicta, cuius sepulcrum in parte Syrtium Maiorum est.
pairs.question: A quo rege gentem Psyllorum in Africa nomen accepisse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: From which king does Pliny say the African people of the Psylli took their name?
pairs.derivation: The Psylli, the famous snake-charming people of the Syrtes, named from king Psyllus whose tomb lies by the Greater Syrtis. Anchored to the named people; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Psylli are a stock reference for snake-immunity in Latin literature.

pairs.source_text: horum corpori ingenitum fuit virus exitiale serpentibus et cuius odore sopirent eas; mos vero liberos genitos protinus obiciendi saevissimis earum eoque genere pudicitiam coniugum experiendi, non profugientibus adulterino sanguine natos serpentibus.
pairs.question: Quo more Psylli pudicitiam coniugum suarum experiri solebant?
pairs.question_en: By what custom did the Psylli test the chastity of their wives?
pairs.answer_en: By exposing their newborn children to snakes.
pairs.derivation: The Psyllan ordeal: infants were thrown to the fiercest snakes, which fled from children of adulterous blood. Anchored to the named people; the custom is stated verbatim (mos vero liberos genitos protinus obiciendi ... eoque genere pudicitiam coniugum experiendi). A named ethnographic custom, closed-book and short-answerable.

pairs.source_text: simile et in Italia Marsorum genus durat, quos a Circae filio ortos ferunt et ideo inesse iis vim naturalem eam.
pairs.question: A cuius filio Marsos, gentem Italiae serpentibus immunem, ortos esse ferunt?
pairs.question_en: From whose son are the Marsi, the Italian people immune to snakes, said to be descended?
pairs.derivation: The Marsi of central Italy, proverbial snake-handlers, traced to a son of Circe, whence their inborn power against serpents. Anchored to the named people; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Marsian snake-charmers are a commonplace of Roman culture.

pairs.source_text: Haut procul urbe Roma in Faliscorum agro familiae sunt paucae quae vocantur Hirpi. hae sacrificio annuo, quod fit ad montem Soractem Apollini, super ambustam ligni struem ambulantes non aduruntur et ob id perpetuo senatus consulto militiae omniumque aliorum munerum vacationem habent.
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellantur illae Faliscorum agri familiae quae ad montem Soractem super ambustam ligni struem inlaesae ambulant?
pairs.question_en: What are the families of the Faliscan territory called who walk unburned over a heap of charred wood at Mount Soracte?
pairs.derivation: The Hirpi Sorani, the fire-walking families of the Faliscan country. Anchored to the place (ager Faliscus, mons Soracte) and the rite; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a celebrated Italian religious custom.

pairs.source_text: hae sacrificio annuo, quod fit ad montem Soractem Apollini, super ambustam ligni struem ambulantes non aduruntur et ob id perpetuo senatus consulto militiae omniumque aliorum munerum vacationem habent.
pairs.question: Cui deo Hirpi ad montem Soractem sacrificium annuum faciebant?
pairs.question_en: To which god did the Hirpi make their annual sacrifice at Mount Soracte?
pairs.derivation: The annual fire-walking sacrifice of the Hirpi at Soracte was made to Apollo (Soranus). Anchored to the named people and mountain; single named answer supported verbatim. A specific cult fact of Italian religion.

pairs.source_text: hae sacrificio annuo, quod fit ad montem Soractem Apollini, super ambustam ligni struem ambulantes non aduruntur et ob id perpetuo senatus consulto militiae omniumque aliorum munerum vacationem habent.
pairs.question: Quid Hirpis perpetuo senatus consulto ob id sacrificium concessum est?
pairs.question_en: What was granted to the Hirpi by a standing decree of the senate on account of that sacrifice?
pairs.answer_en: Exemption from military service and from all other public duties.
pairs.derivation: The Roman senate granted the fire-walking Hirpi a perpetual exemption from military service and all other munera. Anchored to the named families and the senatus consultum; the privilege is stated verbatim. A concrete institutional privilege, closed-book.

pairs.source_text: quorundam corpori partes nascuntur ad aliqua mirabiles, sicut Pyrro regi pollex in dextro pede, cuius tactu lienosis medebatur. hunc cremari cum reliquo corpore non potuisse tradunt conditumque loculo in templo.
pairs.question: Cuius regis pollex in dextro pede tactu lienosis mederi credebatur?
pairs.question_en: Which king's big toe on his right foot was believed to heal sufferers from the spleen by its touch?
pairs.derivation: The healing thumb-toe of king Pyrrhus, which (Pliny adds) could not be burned with the rest of his body and was laid up in a casket in a temple. Anchored to the named king; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a famous curiosity of the king Rome fought in Italy.

pairs.source_text: philosophos eorum, quos gymnosophistas vocant, ab exortu ad occasum perstare contuentes solem inmobilibus oculis, ferventibus harenis toto die alternis pedibus insistere.
pairs.question: Quo nomine philosophi Indorum, qui a solis exortu ad occasum solem inmobilibus oculis contuentur, appellantur?
pairs.question_en: By what name are those Indian philosophers called who gaze at the sun with unmoving eyes from its rising to its setting?
pairs.derivation: The Indian gymnosophistae ('naked philosophers'), a fixture of Greco-Roman accounts of India since Alexander. Anchored to India and the described practice; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book shared knowledge of the ancient world.

pairs.source_text: idem hominum genus, qui Monocoli vocarentur, singulis cruribus, mirae pernicitatis ad saltum; eodem Sciapodas vocari, quod in maiore aestu humi iacentes resupini umbra se pedum protegant.
pairs.question: Quo altero nomine Monocoli, gens Indiae singulis cruribus praedita, propter umbram pedum vocantur?
pairs.question_en: By what other name are the Monocoli, the one-legged Indian people, called, from the shade of their feet?
pairs.derivation: The one-legged Monocoli, also called Sciapodes because they shelter under the shadow of their single foot. Anchored to the named people; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Sciapodes are among the best-known marvels of ancient India-lore.

pairs.source_text: ad extremos fines Indiae ab oriente circa fontem Gangis Astomorum gentem sine ore, corpore toto hirtam vestiri frondium lanugine, halitu tantum viventem et odore, quem naribus trahant.
pairs.question: Qua re sola Astomi, gens Indiae sine ore, vivere dicuntur?
pairs.question_en: On what alone are the Astomi, the mouthless Indian people, said to live?
pairs.derivation: The mouthless Astomi at the source of the Ganges, who live only by breathing in odours. Anchored to the named people and place; the answer is stated verbatim (halitu tantum viventem et odore). Closed-book marvel-ethnography.

pairs.source_text: super hos extrema in parte montium Trispithami Pygmaeique narrantur, ternas spithamas longitudine, hoc est ternos dodrantes, non excedentes, salubri caelo semperque vernante montibus ab aquilone oppositis, quos a gruibus infestari Homerus quoque prodidit.
pairs.question: A quibus avibus Pygmaeos infestari Homerus quoque prodidit?
pairs.question_en: By what birds does Homer too report that the Pygmies are harassed?
pairs.derivation: The war of the Pygmies with the cranes, already in Homer (Iliad 3.3-6) and repeated by Pliny. Anchored to the Pygmies and Homer; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and among the most familiar images of ancient legend.

pairs.source_text: Tergeminos nasci certum est Horatiorum Curiatiorumque exemplo.
pairs.question: Quorum exemplo tergeminos nasci certum esse Plinius adfirmat?
pairs.question_en: By whose example does Pliny affirm it certain that triplets are born?
pairs.answer_en: By that of the Horatii and the Curiatii.
pairs.derivation: Pliny cites the two sets of triplets of Roman legend, the Horatii and Curiatii, as proof that triplets occur. Anchored to the named families; the answer is stated verbatim. Closed-book: the combat of the three Horatii and three Curiatii under Tullus Hostilius is foundational Roman lore.

pairs.source_text: Pompeius Magnus in ornamentis theatri mirabiles fama posuit effigies, ob id diligentius magnorum artificum ingeniis elaboratas, inter quas legitur Eutychis a XX liberis rogo inlata Trallibus, enixa XXX partus.
pairs.question: Quot partus Eutychis Trallibus enixa esse in Pompei theatri ornamentis legebatur?
pairs.question_en: How many times had Eutychis of Tralles given birth, according to the record among the ornaments of Pompey's theatre?
pairs.derivation: Among the marvel-statues in Pompey's theatre stood Eutychis of Tralles, carried to the pyre by twenty children after thirty deliveries. Anchored to the named woman, her city, and Pompey's theatre; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a striking piece of Roman public display.

pairs.source_text: In pedes procidere nascentem contra naturam est, quo argumento eos appellavere Agrippas ut aegri partus, qualiter et M. Agrippam ferunt genitum, unico prope felicitatis exemplo in omnibus ad hunc modum genitis.
pairs.question: Quo nomine ii appellabantur qui in pedes procidentes nascerentur, ut Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: What name was given to those born feet first, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's derivation of the name Agrippa from breech birth (aegre partus), illustrated by M. Agrippa himself. Anchored to the custom and to Agrippa; single answer supported verbatim. Translatable (the answer is a Roman name, not a linguistic trick) and closed-book.

pairs.source_text: ritus naturae hominem capite gigni, mos est pedibus efferri.
pairs.question: Qua corporis parte praeeunte mortuos efferri mos apud Romanos erat, ut Plinius adnotat?
pairs.question_en: With which part of the body going first was it the Roman custom to carry out the dead, as Pliny notes?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's antithesis: nature's rule is to be born head first, custom's rule is to be carried out for burial feet first. Anchored to Roman funeral custom; the answer is stated verbatim (mos est pedibus efferri). A well-known Roman burial usage, closed-book and short-answerable.

pairs.source_text: Auspicatius enecta parente gignuntur, sicut Scipio Africanus prior natus primusque Caesarum a caeso matris utero dictus, qua de causa et Caesones appellati.
pairs.question: Unde primum Caesarum nomen accepisse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: From what does Pliny say the first of the Caesars got his name?
pairs.answer_en: From his mother's womb having been cut open.
pairs.derivation: Pliny's etymology of the cognomen Caesar (and of Caeso) from birth by cutting the mother's womb, alongside the elder Scipio Africanus. Anchored to the Caesares; the answer is stated verbatim. A famous piece of Roman onomastic tradition, translatable as a fact about the name's origin.

pairs.source_text: Vopiscos appellabant e geminis qui retenti utero nascerentur altero interempto abortu.
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellabatur is e geminis qui in utero retentus nasceretur altero abortu interempto?
pairs.question_en: What name was given to the twin who was carried to term after the other had been lost by miscarriage?
pairs.derivation: The Roman term Vopiscus for the surviving twin of a miscarried pair (whence the cognomen). Anchored to the named Roman usage; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman terminology of birth, translatable because the answer is a name.

pairs.source_text: item alii aliaeque feminas tantum generant aut mares, plerumque et alternant, sicut Gracchorum mater duodeciens et Agrippina Germanici noviens.
pairs.question: Quotiens Cornelia, Gracchorum mater, peperisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many times does Pliny report that Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi, gave birth?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's figure for the fecundity of Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi (twelve deliveries), beside Agrippina's nine. Anchored to the named woman; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cornelia and her children are a Roman byword.

pairs.source_text: item alii aliaeque feminas tantum generant aut mares, plerumque et alternant, sicut Gracchorum mater duodeciens et Agrippina Germanici noviens.
pairs.question: Quotiens Agrippina, Germanici uxor, peperisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many times does Pliny report that Agrippina, the wife of Germanicus, gave birth?
pairs.derivation: The elder Agrippina's nine deliveries, cited by Pliny beside Cornelia's twelve. Anchored to the named woman (Germanici); single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and part of the well-known dynastic record of the Julio-Claudians.

pairs.source_text: Q. Metellus Macedonicus, cum sex liberos relinqueret, XI nepotes reliquit, nurus vero generosque et omnes, qui se patris appellatione salutarent, XXVII.
pairs.question: Quot liberos Q. Metellus Macedonicus moriens reliquisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many children does Pliny say Q. Metellus Macedonicus left at his death?
pairs.derivation: The domestic felicity of Metellus Macedonicus: six children, eleven grandchildren, twenty-seven persons who greeted him as father. Anchored to the named consular; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, a stock Roman example of family fortune.

pairs.source_text: nam in viris Masinissam regem post LXXXVI annum generasse filium, quem Methimannum appellaverit, clarum est, Catonem censorium octogensimo exacto e filia Salonis clientis sui.
pairs.question: Post quotum aetatis annum Masinissam regem filium genuisse Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: After what year of his life does Pliny say king Masinissa fathered a son?
pairs.derivation: Masinissa of Numidia fathered a son (Methimannus) after his 86th year. Anchored to the named king; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Masinissa's long-lived vigour is a standard ancient exemplum.

pairs.source_text: nam in viris Masinissam regem post LXXXVI annum generasse filium, quem Methimannum appellaverit, clarum est, Catonem censorium octogensimo exacto e filia Salonis clientis sui.
pairs.question: Ex cuius filia Cato censorius octogesimo aetatis anno exacto filium genuit?
pairs.question_en: By whose daughter did Cato the Censor father a son after completing his eightieth year?
pairs.answer_en: By the daughter of his client Salonius.
pairs.derivation: Cato the Elder's late second marriage to the daughter of his client Salonius, whence the Saloniani branch (from which Cato Uticensis came). Anchored to Cato censorius; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and famous in Roman family history.

pairs.source_text: qua de causa aliorum eius liberum propago Liciniani sunt cognominati, hi Saloniani, ex quis Uticensis fuit.
pairs.question: Ex qua Catonum propagine, Licinianorum an Salonianorum, Cato Uticensis ortus est?
pairs.question_en: From which branch of the Catos, the Liciniani or the Saloniani, did Cato of Utica descend?
pairs.derivation: Pliny distinguishes the two lines of Cato the Elder's descendants, Liciniani and Saloniani, and places Cato Uticensis in the latter. Anchored to the named branches and to Cato Uticensis; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman genealogy.

pairs.source_text: quosdam et cum dentibus nasci, sicut M'. Curium, qui ob id Dentatus cognominatus est, et Cn. Papirium Carbonem, praeclaros viros.
pairs.question: Ob quam causam M'. Curius cognomen Dentati accepit, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: For what reason, according to Pliny, did Manius Curius receive the surname Dentatus?
pairs.answer_en: Because he was born with teeth.
pairs.derivation: Pliny explains the cognomen of M'. Curius Dentatus, victor over Pyrrhus, by birth with teeth already grown. Anchored to the named Roman; short causal answer that is a plain fact, supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman onomastics.

pairs.source_text: Hominem prius quam genito dente cremari mos gentium non est.
pairs.question: Quales infantes cremari mos gentium non erat, ut Plinius adnotat?
pairs.question_en: Which infants, as Pliny notes, it was not the custom of nations to cremate?
pairs.answer_en: Those who had not yet cut a tooth.
pairs.derivation: The rule that a child who had not yet cut a tooth was not cremated but buried. Anchored to the funeral custom itself as reported by Pliny; the answer is stated verbatim. A concrete, checkable point of ancient burial practice, closed-book.

pairs.source_text: Risisse eodem die quo genitus esset unum hominum accepimus Zoroastren; eidem cerebrum ita palpitasse, ut inpositam repelleret manum, futurae praesagio scientiae.
pairs.question: Quem unum hominum eodem die quo natus est risisse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who alone of men, according to Pliny, laughed on the very day he was born?
pairs.derivation: The prodigy of Zoroaster laughing at birth, a portent of his coming wisdom. Anchored to the named figure; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Zoroaster's birth-laugh is a widely repeated ancient tradition.

pairs.source_text: Orestis corpus oraculi iussu refossum VII cubitorum fuisse monumentis creditur.
pairs.question: Quot cubitorum corpus Orestis oraculi iussu refossum fuisse creditur?
pairs.question_en: How many cubits long was the body of Orestes believed to be when it was dug up at the oracle's command?
pairs.derivation: The disinterment of Orestes' seven-cubit body at Delphi's command (cf. Herodotus 1.68). Anchored to Orestes and the oracle; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book heroic lore.

pairs.source_text: procerissimum hominum aetas nostra Divo Claudio principe Gabbaram nomine ex Arabia advectum novem pedum et totidem unciarum vidit.
pairs.question: Quo nomine fuit homo procerissimus, ex Arabia advectus, quem Plinii aetas Claudio principe vidit?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of the tallest man, brought from Arabia, whom Pliny's own age saw in the principate of Claudius?
pairs.derivation: Gabbara, the nine-foot-nine giant brought from Arabia under Claudius, the tallest man of Pliny's day. Anchored to the reign and the man; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book curiosity of imperial Rome.

pairs.source_text: eodem praeside minimus homo duos pedes et palmum Conopas nomine in deliciis Iuliae neptis eius fuit, et mulier Andromeda, liberta Iuliae Augustae.
pairs.question: Quo nomine fuit minimus homo, duos pedes et palmum longus, qui in deliciis Iuliae, Augusti neptis, fuit?
pairs.question_en: What was the name of the smallest man, two feet and a palm high, who was a favourite of Julia, Augustus's granddaughter?
pairs.derivation: The dwarf Conopas, pet of the younger Julia, beside the freedwoman Andromeda. Anchored to Julia and Augustus's court; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book detail of Roman court life (delicia).

pairs.source_text: Ferunt Crassum, avum Crassi in Parthis interempti, numquam risisse, ob id Agelastum vocatum, sicuti nec flesse multos.
pairs.question: Cur Crassus, avus eius Crassi qui in Parthis interemptus est, Agelastus vocatus est?
pairs.question_en: Why was Crassus, the grandfather of the Crassus killed among the Parthians, called Agelastus?
pairs.derivation: The cognomen Agelastus ('never-laughing') of the grandfather of the triumvir Crassus. Anchored by the named descendant killed at Carrhae; short answer stated verbatim. Closed-book Roman anecdote (also in Cicero, Tusc. 3.31).

pairs.source_text: Milonem athletam, cum constitisset, nemo vestigio educebat, malum tenenti modo digitum corrigebat.
pairs.question: Quem athletam, cum constitisset, nemo loco movere poterat, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which athlete, once he had taken his stance, could no one shift from the spot, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Milo of Croton's immovable stance and unbendable finger, the standard ancient emblem of strength. Anchored to the named athlete; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and thoroughly ambient.

pairs.source_text: Cucurrisse MCXL stadia ab Athenis Lacedaemonem biduo Philippidem magnum erat, donec Anystis cursor Lacedaemonius et Philonides Alexandri Magni a Sicyone Elim uno die MCCCV cucurrerunt.
pairs.question: Quot stadia Philippides ab Athenis Lacedaemonem biduo cucurrisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many stades is Philippides said to have run from Athens to Sparta in two days?
pairs.derivation: The run of Philippides from Athens to Sparta, 1,140 stades in two days. Anchored to the named runner and the two cities; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the most famous long run of antiquity.

pairs.source_text: donec Anystis cursor Lacedaemonius et Philonides Alexandri Magni a Sicyone Elim uno die MCCCV cucurrerunt.
pairs.question: Quot stadia Anystis Lacedaemonius et Philonides a Sicyone Elim uno die cucurrerunt?
pairs.question_en: How many stades did Anystis the Spartan and Philonides run from Sicyon to Elis in a single day?
pairs.derivation: The record that surpassed Philippides: 1,305 stades from Sicyon to Elis in one day, by Anystis and by Philonides, Alexander's courier. Anchored to the named runners and route; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book record-fact.

pairs.source_text: si quis cogitet nocte ac die longissimum iter vehiculis Tib. Neronem emensum festinantem ad Drusum fratrem aegrotum in Germaniam. ea fuerunt CC passuum.
pairs.question: Ad quem fratrem aegrotum in Germaniam festinans Tiberius Nero longissimum iter nocte ac die vehiculis emensus est?
pairs.question_en: To which sick brother in Germany was Tiberius Nero hurrying when he covered the longest journey by carriage in a night and a day?
pairs.derivation: Tiberius's celebrated dash of 200 miles by carriage to the dying Drusus in Germany. Anchored to the two named brothers; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a well-known episode of the Augustan house.

pairs.source_text: in nuce inclusam Iliadem Homeri carmen in membrana scriptum tradit Cicero.
pairs.question: Quod Homeri carmen in membrana scriptum et in nuce inclusum fuisse Cicero tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which poem of Homer does Cicero report to have been written on parchment and enclosed in a nutshell?
pairs.derivation: The 'Iliad in a nutshell', reported by Cicero and repeated by Pliny among marvels of eyesight and craft. Anchored to Homer and Cicero; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and proverbially famous.

pairs.source_text: huic et nomen M. Varro reddit: Strabonem vocatum; solitum autem Punico bello a Lilybaeo Siciliae promunturio, exeunte classe e Carthaginis portu, etiam numerum navium dicere.
pairs.question: Quis, ut M. Varro tradit, Punico bello a Lilybaeo promunturio numerum navium e Carthaginis portu exeuntium dicere solebat?
pairs.question_en: Who, as Varro records, used in the Punic War to count from the promontory of Lilybaeum the ships leaving the harbour of Carthage?
pairs.derivation: The far-sighted Strabo, named by Varro, who could see 135 miles and count the Carthaginian fleet from Lilybaeum. Anchored to Varro, Lilybaeum, and Carthage; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book marvel of the senses.

pairs.source_text: Myrmecides quidem in eodem genere inclaruit quadriga ex eadem materia, quam musca integeret alis, fabricata et nave, quam apicula pinnis absconderet.
pairs.question: Quo opere ex ebore facto Myrmecides inclaruit, quod musca alis integere posset?
pairs.question_en: By what ivory work, which a fly could cover with its wings, did Myrmecides become famous?
pairs.derivation: Myrmecides' ivory quadriga small enough for a fly's wings to hide, the companion marvel to Callicrates' ivory ants. Anchored to the named craftsman; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Myrmecides and Callicrates are the ancient byword for miniature art.

pairs.source_text: Auditus unum exemplum habet mirabile proelium, quo Sybaris deleta est, eo die quo gestum erat auditum Olympiae.
pairs.question: Ubi proelium, quo Sybaris deleta est, eodem die quo gestum est auditum esse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Where is the battle in which Sybaris was destroyed said to have been heard on the very day it was fought?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's single marvel of hearing: the destruction of Sybaris heard at Olympia the same day. Anchored to Sybaris; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and tied to two famous Greek names.

pairs.source_text: nam fama Cimbricae victoriae Castoresque, Romam qui Persicam victoriam ipso die quo contigit nuntiavere, visus et numinum fuere praesagia.
pairs.question: Qui dei Romam Persicam victoriam ipso die quo contigit nuntiavisse feruntur?
pairs.question_en: Which gods are said to have announced the victory over Perseus at Rome on the very day it was won?
pairs.derivation: The Dioscuri bringing news of Pydna to Rome the same day, a canonical Roman prodigy. Anchored to Rome and the Persica victoria; single answer supported verbatim (Castores). Closed-book and central to the cult of Castor and Pollux at Rome.

pairs.source_text: Patientia corporis, ut est crebra sors calamitatium, innumera documenta peperit, clarissimum in feminis Leaenae meretricis, quae torta non indicavit Harmodium et Aristogitonem tyrannicidas.
pairs.question: Quae meretrix, tormentis subiecta, Harmodium et Aristogitonem tyrannicidas non prodidit?
pairs.question_en: Which courtesan, under torture, did not betray the tyrannicides Harmodius and Aristogiton?
pairs.derivation: Leaena's silence under torture in the Athenian tyrannicide story. Anchored to Harmodius and Aristogiton; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, part of the shared Athenian legend.

pairs.source_text: in viris Anaxarchi, qui, simili de causa cum torqueretur, praerosam dentibus linguam unamque spem indicii in tyranni os expuit.
pairs.question: Quis philosophus, cum torqueretur, linguam dentibus praerosam in tyranni os expuit?
pairs.question_en: Which philosopher, while being tortured, bit off his tongue and spat it in the tyrant's face?
pairs.derivation: Anaxarchus of Abdera biting off his tongue under torture, Pliny's male counterpart to Leaena. Anchored to the named philosopher; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a standard exemplum of endurance.

pairs.source_text: Cyrus rex omnibus in exercitu suo militibus nomina reddidit, L. Scipio populo Romano, Cineas Pyrrhi regis legatus senatui et equestri ordini Romae postero die quam advenerat.
pairs.question: Quis rex omnibus in exercitu suo militibus nomina reddidisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Which king, according to Pliny, could give back the names of all the soldiers in his army?
pairs.derivation: Cyrus's prodigious memory for the names of his whole army, first in Pliny's list of memory-feats. Anchored to the named king; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a stock example (cf. Cicero, Sen. 21).

pairs.source_text: Cineas Pyrrhi regis legatus senatui et equestri ordini Romae postero die quam advenerat.
pairs.question: Cuius regis legatus Cineas fuit, qui postero die quam Romam advenerat senatui et equestri ordini nomina reddidit?
pairs.question_en: Whose ambassador was Cineas, who the day after his arrival at Rome could name the whole senate and equestrian order?
pairs.derivation: Cineas, envoy of Pyrrhus, learned the names of the senate and equites in a day. Anchored to the named envoy and Rome; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a celebrated Roman anecdote.

pairs.source_text: ictus lapide oblitus est litteras tantum; ex praealto tecto lapsus matris et adfinium propinquorumque cepit oblivionem, alius aegrotus servorum, etiam sui vero nominis Messala Corvinus orator.
pairs.question: Quis orator, ut Plinius tradit, etiam sui nominis oblitus est?
pairs.question_en: Which orator, according to Pliny, forgot even his own name?
pairs.derivation: The Augustan orator M. Valerius Messala Corvinus lost the memory of his own name in illness, Pliny's extreme case of memory's fragility. Anchored to the named orator; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

pairs.source_text: scribere aut legere, simul dictare et audire solitum accepimus, epistulas vero tantarum rerum quaternas pariter dictare.
pairs.question: Quot epistulas de rebus maximis Caesarem dictatorem pariter dictare solitum esse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: How many letters on affairs of the greatest importance does Pliny say Caesar the dictator used to dictate at one time?
pairs.derivation: Caesar's celebrated mental speed: reading or writing while dictating and listening, and dictating four letters at once. Anchored to Caesar; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a stock illustration of Caesar's capacity.

pairs.source_text: idem signis conlatis bis et quinquagiens dimicavit, solus M. Marcellum transgressus, qui undequadragiens dimicavit.
pairs.question: Quotiens Caesar dictator signis conlatis dimicavisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many pitched battles does Pliny say Caesar the dictator fought?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's count of Caesar's pitched battles (52), which alone surpassed Marcellus's 39. Anchored to Caesar; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book record-fact of Roman military history.

pairs.source_text: idem signis conlatis bis et quinquagiens dimicavit, solus M. Marcellum transgressus, qui undequadragiens dimicavit.
pairs.question: Quotiens M. Marcellus signis conlatis dimicavit, quem solus Caesar numero proeliorum transgressus est?
pairs.question_en: How many pitched battles did M. Marcellus fight, whose record Caesar alone surpassed?
pairs.derivation: Marcellus's 39 pitched battles, the record before Caesar. Anchored to the named commander; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and part of the Roman canon of military records.

pairs.source_text: nam praeter civiles victorias undeciens centena et nonaginta duo milia hominum occisa proeliis ab eo non equidem in gloria posuerim.
pairs.question: Quot hominum milia, praeter civiles victorias, proeliis a Caesare occisa esse Plinius scribit?
pairs.answer: Undeciens centena et nonaginta duo milia.
pairs.question_en: How many men, apart from his victories in the civil wars, does Pliny say were killed in battle by Caesar?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's figure of 1,192,000 killed in Caesar's battles, which he pointedly refuses to count as glory. Anchored to Caesar; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a much-quoted statistic.

pairs.source_text: illa fuit vera et incomparabilis invicti animi sublimitas, captis apud Pharsaliam Pompei Magni scriniis epistularum iterumque apud Thapsum Scipionis concremasse ea optima fide atque non legisse.
pairs.question: Quid Caesar cum scriniis epistularum apud Pharsaliam et apud Thapsum captis fecit?
pairs.question_en: What did Caesar do with the letter-cases captured at Pharsalus and at Thapsus?
pairs.answer_en: He burned them without reading them.
pairs.derivation: Caesar burned Pompey's and Scipio's captured correspondence unread, Pliny's chosen proof of his magnanimity. Anchored to the two named battles and Caesar; short factual answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and famous.

pairs.source_text: eques Romanus, id quod antea nemo, curru triumphali revectus et statim ad solis occasum transgressus, excitatis in Pyrenaeo tropaeis, oppida DCCCLXXVI ab Alpibus ad fines Hispaniae ulterioris in dicionem redacta victoriae suae adscripsit.
pairs.question: Quis primus eques Romanus curru triumphali revectus est, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first Roman knight to ride in a triumphal chariot, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Pompey triumphed as a mere eques, a thing no one had done before (id quod antea nemo). The subject is fixed by the surrounding narrative of Pompey's triumphs (Magni nomine ... capto). Single named answer; closed-book and a famous constitutional oddity of Pompey's career.

pairs.source_text: oppida DCCCLXXVI ab Alpibus ad fines Hispaniae ulterioris in dicionem redacta victoriae suae adscripsit et maiore animo Sertorium tacuit.
pairs.question: Quot oppida ab Alpibus ad fines Hispaniae ulterioris in dicionem redacta Pompeius victoriae suae adscripsit?
pairs.question_en: How many towns from the Alps to the borders of Further Spain did Pompey claim to have brought under Roman control?
pairs.derivation: Pompey's Spanish tally of 876 towns, on the trophies of the Pyrenees. Anchored to Pompey and the Alps-to-Spain span; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and part of Pompey's much-publicized record.

pairs.source_text: hos ergo honores urbi tribuit in delubro Minervae, quod ex manubiis dicabat: CN·POMPEIVS MAGNVS IMPERATOR BELLO XXX ANNORVM CONFECTO FVSIS FVGATIS OCCISIS IN DEDITIONEM ACCEPTIS HOMINVM CENTIENS VICIENS SEMEL LXXXIII DEPRESSIS AVT CAPTIS NAVIBVS DCCCXLVI OPPIDIS CASTELLIS MDXXXVIII IN FIDEM RECEPTIS TERRIS A MAEOTIS AD RVBRVM MARE SVBACTIS VOTVM MERITO MINERVAE.
pairs.question: Cui deae Cn. Pompeius Magnus delubrum ex manubiis dicavit, in quo titulos victoriarum suarum posuit?
pairs.question_en: To which goddess did Pompey the Great dedicate, from his spoils, the shrine in which he set the record of his victories?
pairs.derivation: Pompey's dedication ex manubiis to Minerva, closing with VOTVM MERITO MINERVAE. Anchored to Pompey and the shrine; single named answer supported verbatim by the quoted inscription. Closed-book: a famous Roman victory-dedication.

pairs.source_text: CN·POMPEIVS MAGNVS IMPERATOR BELLO XXX ANNORVM CONFECTO FVSIS FVGATIS OCCISIS IN DEDITIONEM ACCEPTIS HOMINVM CENTIENS VICIENS SEMEL LXXXIII DEPRESSIS AVT CAPTIS NAVIBVS DCCCXLVI OPPIDIS CASTELLIS MDXXXVIII IN FIDEM RECEPTIS TERRIS A MAEOTIS AD RVBRVM MARE SVBACTIS VOTVM MERITO MINERVAE.
pairs.question: Quot oppida castellaque in fidem recepta Pompeius Magnus in titulo Minervae dicato numeravit?
pairs.question_en: How many towns and forts taken into surrender did Pompey record on his dedication to Minerva?
pairs.derivation: The figure OPPIDIS CASTELLIS MDXXXVIII from Pompey's dedicatory inscription. Anchored to Pompey and the inscription; single number answer quoted verbatim. Closed-book: this inscription is the canonical summary of Pompey's eastern conquests.

pairs.source_text: triumphi vero, quem duxit a. d. III kal. Oct. M. Pisone M. Messala cos., praefatio haec fuit: CVM ORAM MARITIMAM PRAEDONIBVS LIBERASSET ET IMPERIVM MARIS POPVLO ROMANO RESTITVISSET EX ASIA PONTO ARMENIA PAPHLAGONIA CAPPADOCIA CILICIA SYRIA SCYTHIS IVDAEIS ALBANIS HIBERIA INSVLA CRETA BASTERNIS ET SVPER HAEC DE REGE MITHRIDATE ATQVE TIGRANE TRIVMPHAVIT.
pairs.question: De quibus duobus regibus Cn. Pompeius Magnus in triumpho suo orientali triumphasse in titulo scriptum est?
pairs.question_en: Over which two kings does the inscription say Pompey the Great triumphed in his eastern triumph?
pairs.derivation: The preamble of Pompey's third triumph names the two kings, Mithridates and Tigranes. Anchored to Pompey and the recorded triumph; the answer is quoted verbatim. Closed-book and central to the history of the Mithridatic wars.

pairs.source_text: Cato primus Porciae gentis tres summas in homine res praestitisse existimatur, ut esset optimus orator, optimus imperator, optimus senator.
pairs.question: Quas tres summas res Catonem censorium praestitisse existimatur?
pairs.answer: Ut esset optimus orator, optimus imperator, optimus senator.
pairs.question_en: Which three supreme distinctions is Cato the Censor held to have achieved?
pairs.answer_en: To be the best orator, the best general, and the best senator.
pairs.derivation: The fixed triad by which Cato the Elder was praised. Anchored to Cato primus Porciae gentis; the three-part answer is a set formula quoted verbatim, not a list of interchangeable items. Closed-book and a standard Roman judgment on Cato.

pairs.source_text: itaque sit proprium Catonis quater et quadragiens causam dixisse, nec quemquam saepius postulatum et semper absolutum.
pairs.question: Quotiens Cato censorius causam dixit, semper absolutus?
pairs.question_en: How many times did Cato the Censor stand trial, always acquitted?
pairs.derivation: Cato was prosecuted 44 times and acquitted every time — more often than anyone. Anchored to Cato; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a celebrated fact of his career.

pairs.source_text: Q. Ennius T. Caecilium Teucrum fratremque eius praecipue miratus propter eos sextum decimum adiecit annalem.
pairs.question: Quorum virtutem miratus Q. Ennius sextum decimum annalem adiecit?
pairs.question_en: Whose valour so impressed Ennius that he added a sixteenth book to his Annals?
pairs.answer_en: That of T. Caecilius Teucer and his brother.
pairs.derivation: Pliny's explanation of the added sixteenth book of Ennius's Annales. Anchored to Ennius and the named brothers; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Latin literary history.

pairs.source_text: L. Siccius Dentatus, qui tribunus plebei fuit Sp. Tarpeio A. Aternio cos. haud multo post exactos reges, vel numerosissima suffragia habet centiens viciens proeliatus, octiens ex provocatione victor, quadraginta quinque cicatricibus adverso corpore insignis, nulla in tergo.
pairs.question: Quot cicatrices adverso corpore L. Siccius Dentatus habuit, nulla in tergo?
pairs.question_en: How many scars did L. Siccius Dentatus bear on the front of his body, and none on his back?
pairs.derivation: Siccius Dentatus, the 'Roman Achilles', with 45 scars all in front. Anchored to the named tribune; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Siccius is the standard Roman exemplum of a decorated soldier.

pairs.source_text: L. Siccius Dentatus, qui tribunus plebei fuit Sp. Tarpeio A. Aternio cos. haud multo post exactos reges, vel numerosissima suffragia habet centiens viciens proeliatus, octiens ex provocatione victor.
pairs.question: Quotiens L. Siccius Dentatus in proelio pugnavisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: In how many battles is L. Siccius Dentatus said to have fought?
pairs.derivation: Siccius Dentatus fought 120 battles and won eight single combats. Anchored to the named tribune; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman record of valour.

pairs.source_text: idem spolia cepit XXXIIII, donatus hastis puris duodeviginti, phaleris viginti quinque, torquibus tribus et octoginta, armillis CLX, coronis XXVI, in iis civicis XIIII, aureis octo, muralibus tribus, obsidionali una.
pairs.question: Quot coronas civicas L. Siccius Dentatus inter viginti sex coronas meruit?
pairs.question_en: How many civic crowns, out of twenty-six crowns in all, did L. Siccius Dentatus win?
pairs.derivation: The tally of Siccius's decorations, including 14 coronae civicae among 26 crowns. Anchored to the named soldier and the corona civica (the crown for saving a citizen's life); single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman military honours.

pairs.source_text: primus omnium eques muralem acceperat coronam, sex civicas, XXXVII dona, XXIII cicatrices adverso corpore exceperat, P. Servilium magistrum equitum servaverat, ipse vulneratus umerum, femur.
pairs.question: Quis primus omnium eques coronam muralem accepit, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first knight of all to receive the mural crown, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: M. Manlius Capitolinus, named at the head of the passage (Capitolini decora), was the first eques to win the corona muralis. Anchored to the named Roman and the specific decoration; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman military honours.

pairs.source_text: super omnia Capitolium summamque rem in eo solus a Gallis servaverat, si non regno suo servasset.
pairs.question: Quis solus Capitolium a Gallis servavisse a Plinio dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, alone saved the Capitol from the Gauls?
pairs.derivation: M. Manlius Capitolinus's defence of the Capitol against the Gauls, from which his cognomen came. Anchored to the Capitol and the Gallic attack; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and among the best-known episodes of early Roman history.

pairs.source_text: sinistra manu sola quater pugnavit, uno die duobus equis insidente eo suffossis. dextram sibi ferream fecit eaque religata proeliatus Cremonam obsidione exemit, Placentiam tutatus est, duodena castra hostium in Gallia cepit.
pairs.question: Quis Romanus, amissa dextra manu, ferream sibi fecit eaque religata proeliatus est?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman, having lost his right hand, made himself an iron one and fought with it strapped on?
pairs.derivation: M. Sergius, whom Pliny ranks above all men for courage, fought with an iron right hand after losing his own in the Hannibalic war. Named at 7.104 (M. Sergio ... nemo quemquam hominum iure praetulerit); single named answer supported by the quoted text. Closed-book Roman exemplum.

pairs.source_text: M. Sergio, ut equidem arbitror, nemo quemquam hominum iure praetulerit, licet pronepos Catilina gratiam nomini deroget.
pairs.question: Cuius Romani, quem Plinius fortitudine omnibus praefert, pronepos Catilina fuit?
pairs.question_en: Whose great-grandson was Catiline, the Roman whom Pliny ranks above all others for courage?
pairs.derivation: Pliny notes that Catiline was the great-grandson of the heroic M. Sergius, and that the descendant's name detracts from the ancestor's credit. Anchored to Catiline; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman genealogy.

pairs.source_text: inter spolia Darii Persarum regis unguentorum scrinio capto, quod erat auro, margaritis gemmisque pretiosum, varios eius usus amicis demonstrantibus, quando taedebat unguenti bellatorem et militia sordidum: immo Hercule, inquit, librorum Homeri custodiae detur, ut pretiosissimum humani animi opus quam maxime diviti opere servaretur.
pairs.question: Cui rei Alexander Magnus scrinium unguentorum inter Darii spolia captum destinavit?
pairs.question_en: To what use did Alexander the Great assign the perfume casket captured among the spoils of Darius?
pairs.answer_en: To the keeping of the books of Homer.
pairs.derivation: Alexander's famous saying that Darius's jewelled casket should house Homer. Anchored to Alexander and Darius; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the best-known anecdotes about Alexander and the Iliad.

pairs.source_text: idem Pindari vatis familiae penatibusque iussit parci, cum Thebas raperet, Aristotelis philosophi patriam suam credidit tantaeque rerum claritati tam benignum testimonium miscuit.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae domui et familiae Alexander Magnus parci iussit, cum Thebas everteret?
pairs.question_en: Whose house and family did Alexander the Great order to be spared when he sacked Thebes?
pairs.derivation: Alexander spared the house of Pindar in the destruction of Thebes. Anchored to Alexander and Thebes; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and among the most repeated stories of Alexander's respect for poets.

pairs.source_text: Sophoclem tragici cothurni principem defunctum sepelire Liber pater iussit, obsidentibus moenis Lacedaemoniis, Lysandro eorum rege in quiete saepius admonito ut pateretur humari delicias suas.
pairs.question: Quem tragicum poetam defunctum sepeliri Liber pater, Lysandrum in quiete admonens, iussit?
pairs.question_en: Which tragic poet did Father Liber, warning Lysander repeatedly in his sleep, order to be buried?
pairs.derivation: Dionysus's dream-command to Lysander to allow the burial of Sophocles during the siege of Athens. Anchored to Liber/Dionysus and Lysander; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a canonical story of the poet's death.

pairs.source_text: Archilochi poetae interfectores Apollo arguit Delphis.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae interfectores Apollo Delphis arguit?
pairs.question_en: Whose killers did Apollo denounce at Delphi?
pairs.derivation: The Delphic god's denunciation of the man who killed Archilochus. Anchored to Apollo and Delphi; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, a standard item of Greek literary legend.

pairs.source_text: Platoni sapientiae antistiti Dionysius tyrannus, alias saevitiae superbiaeque natus, vittatam navem misit obviam, ipse quadrigis albis egredientem in litore excepit.
pairs.question: Quem philosophum Dionysius tyrannus navi vittata missa et albis quadrigis in litore excepit?
pairs.question_en: Which philosopher did the tyrant Dionysius welcome with a garlanded ship and with white four-horse chariots on the shore?
pairs.derivation: Dionysius's ceremonial reception of Plato in Sicily. Anchored to Dionysius; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Plato's visits to the Syracusan court are shared knowledge.

pairs.source_text: viginti talentis unam orationem Isocrates vendidit.
pairs.question: Quanti Isocrates unam orationem vendidisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: For how much does Pliny say Isocrates sold a single oration?
pairs.derivation: The price of a single speech by Isocrates. Anchored to the named orator; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a much-cited illustration of what rhetoric could fetch.

pairs.source_text: Thucydiden imperatorem Athenienses in exilium egere, rerum conditorem revocavere, eloquentiam mirati cuius virtutem damnaverant.
pairs.question: Quem Athenienses imperatorem in exilium egerunt, rerum autem scriptorem revocaverunt?
pairs.question_en: Whom did the Athenians drive into exile as a general, but recall as a writer of history?
pairs.derivation: The Athenians banished Thucydides the commander and recalled Thucydides the historian. Anchored to Athens and the double role; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and famous.

pairs.source_text: magnum et Menandro in comico socco testimonium regum Aegypti et Macedoniae contigit classe et per legatos petito, maius ex ipso, regiae fortunae praelata litterarum conscientia.
pairs.question: Quem comicum poetam reges Aegypti et Macedoniae classe et legatis missis ad se arcessere temptaverunt?
pairs.question_en: Which comic poet did the kings of Egypt and Macedon try to summon with a fleet and envoys?
pairs.derivation: Menander declined the invitations of the kings of Egypt and Macedon, preferring his literary life. Anchored to the named poet and kings; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Greek literary history.

pairs.source_text: Cn. Pompeius confecto Mithridatico bello intraturus Posidonii sapientiae professione clari domum forem percuti de more a lictore vetuit et fasces litterarum ianuae summisit is cui se oriens occidensque summiserat.
pairs.question: Cuius philosophi domum intraturus Cn. Pompeius lictorem forem de more percutere vetuit?
pairs.question_en: Whose house was Pompey about to enter when he forbade his lictor to strike the door in the customary way?
pairs.derivation: Pompey lowered his fasces at the door of Posidonius after the Mithridatic war. Anchored to Pompey and the war; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a celebrated Roman gesture of deference to learning.

pairs.source_text: Cato censorius in illa nobili trium sapientiae procerum ab Athenis legatione audito Carneade quam primum legatos eos censuit dimittendos, quoniam illo viro argumentante quid veri esset haut facile discerni posset.
pairs.question: Quo philosopho audito Cato censorius legatos Atheniensium quam primum dimittendos esse censuit?
pairs.question_en: After hearing which philosopher did Cato the Censor move that the Athenian envoys be dismissed as soon as possible?
pairs.derivation: The embassy of the three philosophers to Rome (155 BC) and Cato's alarm at Carneades. Anchored to Cato and the Athenian embassy; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a landmark in the story of Greek philosophy at Rome.

pairs.source_text: prior Africanus Q. Ennii statuam sepulcro suo inponi iussit clarumque illud nomen, immo vero spolium ex tertia orbis parte raptum, in cinere supremo cum poetae titulo legi.
pairs.question: Cuius poetae statuam prior Africanus sepulcro suo inponi iussit?
pairs.question_en: Whose statue did the elder Africanus order to be set upon his own tomb?
pairs.derivation: Scipio Africanus the Elder had a statue of Ennius placed on his tomb. Anchored to the elder Africanus; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and famous in the history of Roman patronage of poets.

pairs.source_text: M. Varronis in bibliotheca, quae prima in orbe ab Asinio Pollione ex manubiis publicata Romae est, unius viventis posita imago est, haut minore, ut equidem reor, gloria, principe oratore et cive ex illa ingeniorum quae tunc fuit multitudine uni hanc coronam dante quam cum eidem Magnus Pompeius piratico ex bello navalem dedit.
pairs.question: Cui Magnus Pompeius ex bello piratico coronam navalem dedit?
pairs.question_en: To whom did Pompey the Great give the naval crown for the war against the pirates?
pairs.derivation: Varro won the corona navalis from Pompey in the pirate war — Pliny pairs it with the honour of his portrait in the first public library. Anchored to Pompey and the pirate war; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact about Rome's most learned man.

pairs.source_text: rursus mortales oraculorum societatem dedere Chiloni Lacedaemonio tria praecepta eius Delphis consecrando aureis litteris, quae sunt haec: nosse se quemque, et nihil nimium cupere, comitemque aeris alieni atque litis esse miseriam.
pairs.question: Cuius Lacedaemonii tria praecepta Delphis aureis litteris consecrata sunt?
pairs.question_en: Whose three precepts, those of a Spartan, were consecrated at Delphi in golden letters?
pairs.derivation: The three maxims of Chilon of Sparta (know thyself; desire nothing to excess; debt and litigation bring misery) inscribed in gold at Delphi. Anchored to Delphi and the Spartan sage; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Chilon is one of the Seven Sages.

pairs.source_text: quin et funus eius, cum victore filio Olympiae expirasset gaudio, tota Graecia prosecuta est.
pairs.question: Quo affectu Chilon Lacedaemonius Olympiae, filio vincente, exspiravit?
pairs.question_en: From what emotion did Chilon of Sparta expire at Olympia when his son was victorious?
pairs.derivation: Chilon died of joy at Olympia on his son's victory, and all Greece attended his funeral. Anchored to Chilon and Olympia; single-word answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the classic 'death from joy' anecdote, repeated by Pliny at 7.180.

pairs.source_text: Divinitas et quaedam caelitum societas nobilissima ex feminis in Sibylla fuit, ex viris in Melampode apud Graecos, apud Romanos in Marcio.
pairs.question: Quem vatem Plinius apud Romanos nobilissimum divinitatis exemplum ponit?
pairs.question_en: Which seer does Pliny name as the noblest Roman instance of communion with the gods?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's triad of prophecy: the Sibyl among women, Melampus among the Greeks, Marcius among the Romans (the vates of the carmina Marciana). Anchored to Rome and the category; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman religious lore.

pairs.source_text: Pudicissima femina semel matronarum sententia iudicata est Sulpicia Paterculi filia, uxor Fulvi Flacci, electa ex centum praeceptis quae simulacrum Veneris ex Sibyllinis libris dedicaret.
pairs.question: Quae femina matronarum sententia pudicissima iudicata est, ut simulacrum Veneris ex Sibyllinis libris dedicaret?
pairs.question_en: Which woman was judged by the matrons' vote the most chaste, to dedicate the statue of Venus prescribed by the Sibylline books?
pairs.derivation: Sulpicia, wife of Fulvius Flaccus, chosen out of a hundred as the most chaste matron to dedicate the image of Venus Verticordia. Anchored to the Sibylline books and the dedication; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman cult history.

pairs.source_text: electa ex centum praeceptis quae simulacrum Veneris ex Sibyllinis libris dedicaret, iterum religionis experimento Claudia inducta Romam deum matre.
pairs.question: Quae matrona, religionis experimento, deum matrem Romam induxit?
pairs.question_en: Which matron, by a test of her piety, brought the Mother of the Gods into Rome?
pairs.derivation: Claudia Quinta's proof of chastity when the Magna Mater was brought to Rome in 204 BC. Anchored to the arrival of the deum mater; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and one of the best-known Roman religious legends.

pairs.source_text: quo miraculo matris salus donata pietati est, ambaeque perpetuis alimentis, et locus ille quidem consecratus deae, C. Quinctio M'. Acilio cos. templo Pietatis extructo in illius carceris sede, ubi nunc Marcelli theatrum est.
pairs.question: Cuius deae templum in eo carceris loco extructum est, ubi filia matrem inclusam lacte suo aluerat?
pairs.question_en: To which goddess was the temple built on the site of the prison where a daughter fed her imprisoned mother with her own milk?
pairs.derivation: The temple of Pietas, raised where the prison stood (later the site of the theatre of Marcellus), commemorating the daughter who nursed her mother. Anchored to the story and the site; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the caritas Romana is a canonical Roman exemplum.

pairs.source_text: Gracchorum pater anguibus prehensis in domo, cum responderetur ipsum victurum alterius sexus interempto: immo vero, inquit, meum necate, Cornelia enim iuvenis est et parere adhuc potest.
pairs.question: Utrum ex anguibus in domo prehensis, marem an feminam, Gracchorum pater necari iussit?
pairs.question_en: Which of the snakes caught in his house, the male or the female, did the father of the Gracchi order to be killed?
pairs.derivation: Tiberius Gracchus, told that killing one snake would cost the life of the corresponding spouse, chose to have the male killed to spare Cornelia. Anchored to the Gracchi's father and the omen; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a stock Roman story of conjugal devotion.

pairs.source_text: astrologia Berosus, cui ob divinas praedictiones Athenienses publice in gymnasio statuam inaurata lingua statuere.
pairs.question: Cui astrologo Athenienses ob divinas praedictiones statuam inaurata lingua in gymnasio posuerunt?
pairs.question_en: To which astronomer did the Athenians publicly set up a statue with a gilded tongue in the gymnasium, for his divine predictions?
pairs.derivation: The Babylonian Berosus honoured at Athens with a gilt-tongued statue. Anchored to Athens and the honour; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Berosus is the standard ancient name for Chaldean astronomy.

pairs.source_text: Hippocrates medicina, qui venientem ab Illyriis pestilentiam praedixit discipulosque ad auxiliandum circa urbes dimisit, quod ob meritum honores illi quos Herculi decrevit Graecia.
pairs.question: Cui medico, quod pestilentiam ab Illyriis venientem praedixerat, Graecia eosdem honores quos Herculi decrevit?
pairs.question_en: To which physician did Greece decree the same honours as to Hercules, for having foretold the plague coming from Illyria?
pairs.derivation: Hippocrates warned of the plague from Illyria and sent out his pupils; Greece voted him Heracles' honours. Anchored to the named physician and Greece; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, the founding story of medicine's prestige.

pairs.source_text: magna et Critobulo fama est extracta Philippi regis oculo sagitta et citra deformitatem oris curata orbitate luminis.
pairs.question: Quis medicus sagittam ex Philippi regis oculo extraxit sine oris deformitate?
pairs.question_en: Which physician drew the arrow from king Philip's eye without disfiguring his face?
pairs.derivation: Critobulus's surgery on Philip II of Macedon, blinded in one eye at Methone. Anchored to Philip and the wound; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a famous case in ancient medicine.

pairs.source_text: summa autem Asclepiadi Prusiensi condita nova secta, spretis legatis et pollicitationibus Mithridatis regis, reperta ratione qua vinum aegris medetur, relato e funere homine et conservato, sed maxime sponsione facta cum fortuna, ne medicus crederetur, si umquam invalidus ullo modo fuisset ipse.
pairs.question: Quis medicus Prusiensis, nova secta condita, legatos et pollicitationes Mithridatis regis sprevit?
pairs.question_en: Which physician of Prusa, founder of a new school, rejected the envoys and offers of king Mithridates?
pairs.derivation: Asclepiades of Prusa, who founded a new medical sect, treated patients with wine, recovered a man from his own funeral, and wagered that he would never fall ill. Anchored to Mithridates and Prusa; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, the most famous Greek physician at Rome.

pairs.source_text: laudatus est et Chersiphron Gnosius aede Ephesi Dianae admirabili fabricata, Philon Athenis armamentario CD navium, Ctesibius pneumatica ratione et hydraulicus organis repertis, Dinochares metatus Alexandro condente in Aegypto Alexandriam.
pairs.question: Quis architectus aedem Dianae Ephesiae fabricavit, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which architect built the temple of Diana at Ephesus, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Chersiphron as builder of the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders. Anchored to the named temple; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of ancient architecture.

pairs.source_text: Ctesibius pneumatica ratione et hydraulicus organis repertis, Dinochares metatus Alexandro condente in Aegypto Alexandriam.
pairs.question: Quis pneumaticam rationem et hydraulica organa repperisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented pneumatics and the water-organ?
pairs.derivation: Ctesibius of Alexandria as inventor of pneumatics and the hydraulic organ. Anchored to the named inventions; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the hydraulis is a well-known ancient instrument.

pairs.source_text: Dinochares metatus Alexandro condente in Aegypto Alexandriam.
pairs.question: Quis architectus Alexandriam Aegypti, condente eam Alexandro, metatus est?
pairs.question_en: Which architect laid out Alexandria in Egypt when Alexander founded it?
pairs.derivation: Deinocrates/Dinochares as the planner of Alexandria at its foundation. Anchored to Alexander and Alexandria; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of city-founding history.

pairs.source_text: idem hic imperator edixit ne quis ipsum alius quam Apelles pingeret, quam Pyrgoteles scalperet, quam Lysippus ex aere duceret.
pairs.question: Cui uni Alexander Magnus edicto permisit ut se ex aere duceret?
pairs.question_en: To whom alone did Alexander the Great grant by edict the right to cast him in bronze?
pairs.derivation: Alexander's edict reserving his bronze portraits to Lysippus (with Apelles for painting and Pyrgoteles for gems). Anchored to Alexander and the medium; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book art history; distinct from the painting fact already taken.

pairs.source_text: idem hic imperator edixit ne quis ipsum alius quam Apelles pingeret, quam Pyrgoteles scalperet, quam Lysippus ex aere duceret.
pairs.question: Cui uni Alexander Magnus edicto permisit ut imaginem suam scalperet?
pairs.question_en: To whom alone did Alexander the Great grant by edict the right to engrave his likeness?
pairs.derivation: The third clause of Alexander's edict: gem-engraving reserved to Pyrgoteles. Anchored to Alexander and the craft; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact about the most celebrated ancient gem-cutter.

pairs.source_text: Aristidis Thebani pictoris unam tabulam centum talentis rex Attalus licitus est, octoginta emit duas Caesar dictator, Mediam et Aiacem Timomachi, in templo Veneris Genetricis dicaturus.
pairs.question: Quanti rex Attalus unam Aristidis Thebani tabulam licitus est?
pairs.question_en: How much did king Attalus bid for a single painting by Aristides of Thebes?
pairs.derivation: Attalus's bid of 100 talents for one picture by Aristides of Thebes. Anchored to the named king and painter; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of the ancient art market.

pairs.source_text: octoginta emit duas Caesar dictator, Mediam et Aiacem Timomachi, in templo Veneris Genetricis dicaturus.
pairs.question: Quas duas Timomachi tabulas Caesar dictator in templo Veneris Genetricis dicaturus emit?
pairs.question_en: Which two paintings by Timomachus did Caesar the dictator buy to dedicate in the temple of Venus Genetrix?
pairs.derivation: Caesar bought Timomachus's Medea and Ajax for 80 talents for his temple of Venus Genetrix. Anchored to Caesar, the painter, and the temple; the two named works are quoted verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman art collecting.

pairs.source_text: Rhodum non incendit rex Demetrius expugnator cognominatus, ne tabulam Protogenis cremaret a parte ea muri locatam.
pairs.question: Cuius pictoris tabulae parcens rex Demetrius Rhodum non incendit?
pairs.question_en: To spare whose painting did king Demetrius refrain from burning Rhodes?
pairs.derivation: Demetrius Poliorcetes spared Rhodes rather than destroy a painting by Protogenes. Anchored to Demetrius and Rhodes; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a canonical story about the power of art.

pairs.source_text: Pretium hominis in servitio geniti maximum ad hanc diem, quod equidem conpeperim, fuit grammaticae artis, Daphnin Attio Pisaurense vendente et M. Scauro principe civitatis IIi DCC licente.
pairs.question: Cuius artis fuit servus Daphnis, pro quo maximum pretium ad Plinii aetatem licitum est?
pairs.question_en: In which art was the slave Daphnis skilled, for whom the highest price down to Pliny's day was bid?
pairs.derivation: The record price for a home-born slave was paid for the grammarian Daphnis, bid by M. Scaurus. Anchored to the named slave and buyer; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: it tells what Romans valued most in a slave.

pairs.source_text: Una feminarum in omni aevo Lampido Lacedaemonia reperitur, quae regis filia, regis uxor, regis mater fuerit, una Berenice, quae filia, soror, mater Olympionicarum.
pairs.question: Quae sola femina regis filia, regis uxor, regis mater fuisse reperitur?
pairs.question_en: Which woman alone is found to have been the daughter, wife, and mother of a king?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's unique instance of a woman thrice royal. Anchored to the named Spartan woman; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book record-fact of the kind Pliny's book seven collects.

pairs.source_text: una Berenice, quae filia, soror, mater Olympionicarum.
pairs.question: Quae sola femina filia, soror et mater Olympionicarum fuit?
pairs.question_en: Which woman alone was the daughter, sister, and mother of Olympic victors?
pairs.derivation: Berenice's unique Olympic pedigree. Anchored to the named woman and the Olympic victories; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Olympic victor-lists are shared Greek knowledge.

pairs.source_text: una familia Curionum, in qua tres continua serie oratores extiterint, una Fabiorum, in qua tres continui principes senatus, M. Fabius Ambustus, Fabius Rullianus filius, Q. Fabius Gurges nepos.
pairs.question: In qua familia tres continui principes senatus fuerunt, M. Fabius Ambustus, Fabius Rullianus, Q. Fabius Gurges?
pairs.question_en: In which family were there three successive leaders of the senate, M. Fabius Ambustus, Fabius Rullianus, and Q. Fabius Gurges?
pairs.derivation: Three generations of Fabii held the princeps senatus in unbroken succession. Anchored to the three named men and the office; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact about one of Rome's great gentes.

pairs.source_text: una familia Curionum, in qua tres continua serie oratores extiterint.
pairs.question: In qua familia tres continua serie oratores extiterunt, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which family, according to Pliny, did three orators arise in unbroken succession?
pairs.answer_en: In the family of the Curiones.
pairs.derivation: The three successive orators of the Curio family, Pliny's unique instance. Anchored to the named family; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman oratorical history.

pairs.source_text: triumphare P. Ventidium de Parthis voluit quidem solum, sed eundem in triumpho Asculano Cn. Pompei duxit puerum, quamquam Masurius auctor est bis in triumpho ductum, Cicero mulionem castrensis furnariae fuisse.
pairs.question: Quis solus de Parthis triumphavit, cum idem puer in triumpho Asculano ductus esset?
pairs.question_en: Who alone triumphed over the Parthians, though he had himself been led as a boy in the Asculan triumph?
pairs.derivation: Ventidius Bassus, led as a captive child in Pompeius Strabo's Asculan triumph, later the only Roman to triumph over the Parthians. Anchored to the named man and the two triumphs; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book reversal-of-fortune exemplum.

pairs.source_text: fuit et Balbus Cornelius maior consul, sed accusatus atque de iure virgarum in eum iudice in consilium misso, primus externorum atque etiam in oceano genitorum usus illo honore, quem maiores Latio quoque negaverint.
pairs.question: Quis primus externorum, atque etiam in oceano genitorum, consulatu functus est?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first foreigner, and one born by the Ocean at that, to hold the consulship?
pairs.derivation: Cornelius Balbus of Gades, the first non-Italian consul. Anchored to the office and the description; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book landmark in the history of Roman citizenship and office-holding.

pairs.source_text: est et L. Fulvius inter insignia exempla, Tusculanorum rebellantium consul, eodemque honore, cum transisset, exornatus confestim a populo Romano, qui solus eodem anno, quo fuerat hostis, Romae triumphavit ex iis quorum consul fuerat.
pairs.question: Quis solus eodem anno quo hostis fuerat Romae triumphavit ex iis quorum consul fuerat?
pairs.question_en: Who alone triumphed at Rome, in the very year in which he had been an enemy, over the people whose consul he had been?
pairs.derivation: L. Fulvius, consul of the rebel Tusculans, changed sides and was at once made Roman consul, triumphing over his former people. Anchored to Tusculum and the named man; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book oddity of early Roman history.

pairs.source_text: Q. Metellus in ea oratione, quam habuit supremis laudibus patris sui L. Metelli pontificis, bis consulis, dictatoris, magistri equitum, XVviri agris dandis, qui plurimos elephantos ex primo Punico bello duxit in triumpho, scriptum reliquit decem maximas res optimasque, in quibus quaerendis sapientes aetatem exigerent, consummasse eum.
pairs.question: Quis plurimos elephantos ex primo Punico bello in triumpho duxit?
pairs.question_en: Who led the greatest number of elephants in triumph from the First Punic War?
pairs.derivation: L. Caecilius Metellus's triumph after Panormus, famous for its elephants. Anchored to the named man and the First Punic War; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a celebrated Roman spectacle.

pairs.source_text: siquidem is Metellus orbam luminibus exegit senectam, amissis incendio, cum Palladium raperet ex aede Vestae, memorabili causa, sed eventu misero.
pairs.question: Qua in re L. Metellus pontifex lumina amisit?
pairs.answer: Palladium ex aede Vestae incendio rapiens.
pairs.question_en: In what act did L. Metellus the pontifex lose his eyesight?
pairs.answer_en: Rescuing the Palladium from the burning temple of Vesta.
pairs.derivation: Metellus was blinded saving the Palladium from the fire in the temple of Vesta (241 BC). Anchored to the named pontifex and the Palladium; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a famous act of Roman piety.

pairs.source_text: tribuit ei populus Romanus quod nulli alii ab condito aevo, ut, quotiens in senatum iret, curru veheretur ad curiam: magnum ei et sublime, sed pro oculis datum.
pairs.question: Quem honorem populus Romanus L. Metello caeco tribuit, quem nulli alii ab condito aevo?
pairs.question_en: What honour did the Roman people grant to the blinded L. Metellus, granted to no one else since the founding of the city?
pairs.answer_en: That he be carried to the senate-house in a chariot.
pairs.derivation: The unique privilege voted to the blind Metellus of riding to the curia. Anchored to the named man and the Roman people; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman public honours.

pairs.source_text: nam praeter honores amplissimos cognomenque Macedonici a quattuor filiis inlatus rogo, uno praetorio, tribus consularibus, duobus triumphalibus, uno censorio, quae singula quoque paucis contigere.
pairs.question: A quot filiis Q. Metellus Macedonicus rogo inlatus est?
pairs.question_en: By how many sons was Q. Metellus Macedonicus carried to his funeral pyre?
pairs.derivation: Metellus Macedonicus was borne to the pyre by four sons, one a praetorian, three consulars, two of them triumphant, one a censor. Anchored to the named man and the funeral; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Roman exemplum of felicitas.

pairs.source_text: in ipso tamen flore dignationis suae ab C. Atinio Labeone, cui cognomen fuit Macerioni, tribuno plebis, quem e senatu censor eiecerat, revertens e campo meridiano tempore vacuo foro et Capitolio ad Tarpeium raptus, ut praecipitaretur.
pairs.question: Quis tribunus plebis Q. Metellum Macedonicum ad Tarpeium rapuit, ut praecipitaretur?
pairs.question_en: Which tribune of the plebs dragged Q. Metellus Macedonicus to the Tarpeian rock to hurl him down?
pairs.derivation: Atinius Labeo, expelled from the senate by the censor Metellus, retaliated by dragging him toward the Tarpeian rock until another tribune interceded. Anchored to both named men; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book episode of censorial and tribunician power.

pairs.source_text: duo sunt haec: Pedium felicissimum, qui pro patria proxime occubuisset; iterum a Gyge rege tunc amplissimo terrarum consulti: Aglaum Psophidium esse feliciorem.
pairs.question: Quem Gygi regi consulenti oraculum Delphicum feliciorem esse respondit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did the Delphic oracle declare happier when king Gyges consulted it?
pairs.derivation: The oracle's rebuke to Gyges: the poor farmer Aglaus of Psophis in Arcadia is happier than the richest king. Anchored to Gyges and Delphi; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a standard moralizing oracle-story.

pairs.source_text: Consecratus est vivus sentiensque eiusdem oraculi iussi et Iovis deorum summi adstipulatu Euthymus pycta, semper Olympiae victor et semel victus. patria ei Locri in Italia; ibi imaginem eius et Olympiae alteram eodem die tactam fulmine Callimachum ut nihil aliud miratum video deumque iussisse sacrificare, quod et vivo factitatum et mortuo.
pairs.question: Quis pycta, Locris in Italia natus, vivus adhuc consecratus est, semper Olympiae victor et semel tantum victus?
pairs.question_en: Which boxer, a native of Locri in Italy, was consecrated while still alive, always victorious at Olympia and beaten only once?
pairs.derivation: Euthymus of Locri, the boxer worshipped as a god in his own lifetime by command of the oracle. Anchored to Locri and Olympia; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a famous case of athletic hero-cult.

pairs.source_text: sed ut ad confessa transeamus, Arganthonium Gaditanum LXXX annis regnasse prope certum est; putant quadragensimo coepisse. Masinissam LX annis regnasse indubitatum est, Gorgian Siculum CVIII vixisse.
pairs.question: Quot annos Arganthonium Gaditanum regnavisse prope certum est?
pairs.question_en: For how many years is it nearly certain that Arganthonius of Gades reigned?
pairs.derivation: Arganthonius, king of Tartessus/Gades, reigned 80 years, beginning at 40. Anchored to the named king; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the type-case of royal longevity in antiquity.

pairs.source_text: Masinissam LX annis regnasse indubitatum est, Gorgian Siculum CVIII vixisse.
pairs.question: Quot annos Masinissam regnavisse indubitatum est?
pairs.question_en: For how many years is it beyond doubt that Masinissa reigned?
pairs.derivation: The sixty-year reign of Masinissa of Numidia, Rome's ally against Carthage. Anchored to the named king; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of the Punic wars' aftermath.

pairs.source_text: Masinissam LX annis regnasse indubitatum est, Gorgian Siculum CVIII vixisse. Q. Fabius Maximus LXIII annis augur fuit.
pairs.question: Quot annos Gorgias Siculus vixisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many years is Gorgias the Sicilian said to have lived?
pairs.derivation: The longevity of Gorgias of Leontini, the sophist. Anchored to the named man; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a familiar fact about the founder of epideictic rhetoric.

pairs.source_text: Q. Fabius Maximus LXIII annis augur fuit.
pairs.question: Quot annos Q. Fabius Maximus augur fuit?
pairs.question_en: For how many years was Q. Fabius Maximus an augur?
pairs.derivation: Fabius Maximus Cunctator held the augurate for 63 years. Anchored to the named man and the priesthood; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact about a lifelong Roman priesthood.

pairs.source_text: M. Valerius Corvinus centum annos inplevit, cuius inter primum et sextum consulatum XLVI anni fuere. idem sella curuli semel ac viciens sedit, quotiens nemo alius.
pairs.question: Quot anni inter primum et sextum M. Valeri Corvini consulatum fuerunt?
pairs.question_en: How many years lay between the first and the sixth consulship of M. Valerius Corvinus?
pairs.derivation: Valerius Corvinus lived a hundred years and held six consulships spanning 46 years. Anchored to the named consul; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of the early Republic's most long-lived magistrate.

pairs.source_text: M. Valerius Corvinus centum annos inplevit, cuius inter primum et sextum consulatum XLVI anni fuere. idem sella curuli semel ac viciens sedit, quotiens nemo alius.
pairs.question: Quotiens M. Valerius Corvinus sella curuli sedit, quotiens nemo alius?
pairs.question_en: How many times did M. Valerius Corvinus hold curule office, more often than anyone else?
pairs.derivation: Corvinus sat in the curule chair twenty-one times, a Roman record. Anchored to the named man and the curule chair; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman office-holding.

pairs.source_text: Et ex feminis Livia Rutili LXXXXVII annos excessit, Statilia Claudio principe ex nobili domo LXXXVIIII, Terentia Ciceronis CIII, Clodia Ofili CXV, haec quidem etiam enixa quindeciens.
pairs.question: Quot annos Terentia, Ciceronis uxor, vixisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many years does Pliny say Terentia, Cicero's wife, lived?
pairs.derivation: Terentia's extraordinary lifespan in Pliny's list of long-lived women. Anchored to Cicero's wife; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and attached to one of the best-known Roman households.

pairs.source_text: Galeria Copiola emboliaria reducta est in scaenam C. Poppaeo Q. Sulpicio cos. ludis pro salute Divi Augusti votivis annum CIIII agens.
pairs.question: Quotum annum agens Galeria Copiola emboliaria in scaenam reducta est ludis pro salute Divi Augusti votivis?
pairs.question_en: In what year of her age was the interlude-dancer Galeria Copiola brought back on stage at the games vowed for the health of the deified Augustus?
pairs.derivation: Galeria Copiola, the emboliaria (interlude performer), returned to the stage at 104. Anchored to the named actress and the votive games; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book detail of the Roman stage.

pairs.source_text: minus miror Stephanionem, qui primus togatus saltare instituit, utrisque saecularibus ludis saltavisse, Divi Augusti et quos Claudius Caesar consulatu suo quarto fecit.
pairs.question: Quis primus togatus saltare instituit, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first to dance in a toga, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Stephanio introduced dancing in the toga (i.e. in Roman dress, the fabula togata), and danced at the Secular Games of both Augustus and Claudius. Anchored to the named performer; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman theatrical history.

pairs.source_text: Q. Fabius Maximus consul apud flumen Isaram proelio commisso adversus Allobrogum Arvernorumque gentes a. d. VI idus Augustas, CXXX perduellium caesis, febri quartana liberatus est in acie.
pairs.question: Apud quod flumen Q. Fabius Maximus consul adversus Allobrogum Arvernorumque gentes proelium commisit?
pairs.question_en: By which river did the consul Q. Fabius Maximus join battle against the Allobroges and the Arverni?
pairs.derivation: Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus's victory at the Isara in 121 BC (Pliny adds that he was cured of a quartan fever in the battle line). Anchored to the named consul and peoples; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Rome's conquest of Transalpine Gaul.

pairs.source_text: ergo pro miraculo et id solitarium reperitur exemplum Xenophili musici, centum et quinque annis vixisse sine ullo corporis incommodo.
pairs.question: Quot annos Xenophilus musicus sine ullo corporis incommodo vixisse traditur?
