pairs.question_en: How many years is Xenophilus the musician said to have lived without any bodily ailment?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's single example of a wholly healthy old age, the musician Xenophilus at 105. Anchored to the named man; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book record-fact.

pairs.source_text: morborum vero tam infinita est multitudo, ut Pherecydes Syrius serpentium multitudine ex corpore eius erumpente expiraverit.
pairs.question: Quo genere mortis Pherecydes Syrius perisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: By what manner of death is Pherecydes of Syros said to have perished?
pairs.answer_en: By a swarm of snakes bursting out of his body.
pairs.derivation: The grotesque death of Pherecydes of Syros, the first prose writer. Anchored to the named philosopher; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a widely repeated ancient tradition about his end.

pairs.source_text: quibusdam perpetua febris est, sicut C. Maecenati; eidem triennio supremo nullo horae momento contigit somnus.
pairs.question: Quo bono C. Maecenas triennio supremo omnino caruisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Of what was Maecenas said to have been entirely deprived in his last three years?
pairs.derivation: Maecenas's chronic fever and total sleeplessness for his last three years. Anchored to the named man; single-word answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a famous detail about Augustus's minister, also known from Seneca.

pairs.source_text: Aviola consularis in rogo revixit et, quoniam subveniri non potuerat praevalente flamma, vivus crematus est. similis causa in L. Lamia praetorio viro traditur.
pairs.question: Quis consularis in rogo revixit et tamen, flamma praevalente, vivus crematus est?
pairs.question_en: Which ex-consul came back to life on the pyre and yet, the flames prevailing, was burned alive?
pairs.derivation: The consular Aviola revived on his own funeral pyre and could not be rescued. Anchored to the named man and the pyre; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a stock horror of Roman cremation practice.

pairs.source_text: Aristeae etiam visam evolantem ex ore in Proconneso corvi effigie, magna quae sequitur hanc fabulositate.
pairs.question: Cuius viri animam Proconnesi corvi effigie ex ore evolare visam esse tradunt?
pairs.question_en: Whose soul is said to have been seen flying from his mouth at Proconnesus in the form of a raven?
pairs.derivation: The soul of Aristeas of Proconnesus leaving his body as a raven. Anchored to the named man and place; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Aristeas is the standard ancient example of soul-travel (cf. Herodotus 4.14-15).

pairs.source_text: quam equidem et in Gnosio Epimenide simili modo accipio, puerum aestu et itinere fessum in specu septem et quinquaginta dormisse annis, rerum faciem mutationemque mirantem velut postero die experrectum.
pairs.question: Quot annos Epimenides Gnosius puer in specu dormivisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many years is Epimenides of Cnossos said to have slept as a boy in a cave?
pairs.derivation: The long sleep of Epimenides of Crete, who woke to find the world changed and lived to 157. Anchored to the named sage; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and among the best-known Greek legends.

pairs.source_text: gaudio obiere praeter Chilonem, de quo diximus, Sophocles et Dionysius Siciliae tyrannus, uterque accepto tragicae victoriae nuntio.
pairs.question: Quo nuntio accepto Sophocles et Dionysius Siciliae tyrannus gaudio obierunt?
pairs.question_en: On receiving news of what did Sophocles and Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, die of joy?
pairs.answer_en: Of a victory in the tragic contest.
pairs.derivation: Both died of joy at news of a prize in the tragic competition. Anchored to the two named men; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the deaths-from-joy catalogue is standard ancient lore, and both men were tragedians.

pairs.source_text: pudore Diodorus sapientiae dialecticae professor, lusoria quaestione non protinus ab interrogatione Stilponis dissoluta.
pairs.question: Cuius interrogatione non statim soluta Diodorus dialecticus pudore obiit?
pairs.question_en: Whose question, left unsolved on the spot, made the dialectician Diodorus die of shame?
pairs.derivation: Diodorus Cronus died of shame at failing to answer Stilpo's puzzle at once. Anchored to both named philosophers; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book anecdote of the dialectical schools.

pairs.source_text: Q. Fabius Maximus in consulatu suo pridie kal. Ian., in cuius locum C. Rebilus paucissimarum horarum consulatum petiit.
pairs.question: Quis in locum Q. Fabi Maximi, pridie kalendas Ianuarias mortui, consulatum paucissimarum horarum petiit?
pairs.question_en: Who sought, in place of Q. Fabius Maximus who died on the last day of December, a consulship of only a few hours?
pairs.derivation: The one-day consulship of Caninius Rebilus in 45 BC, a byword for the debasement of office under Caesar. Anchored to Fabius Maximus's death on the eve of the Kalends; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and famously mocked by Cicero.

pairs.source_text: nulla evidentibus causis obiere, dum calciantur matutino, duo Caesares, praetor et praetura perfunctus dictatoris Caesaris pater — hic Pisis exanimatus est, ille Romae.
pairs.question: In quo oppido pater Caesaris dictatoris, dum mane calciatur, subito exanimatus est?
pairs.question_en: In what town did the father of Caesar the dictator suddenly die while putting on his shoes in the morning?
pairs.derivation: The sudden death of Caesar's father at Pisae while dressing. Anchored to the dictator's father; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book biographical fact (also in Suetonius, Iul. 1).

pairs.source_text: comoediarum histrio is, cum populo admodum placuisset natali die suo conviviumque haberet, edita cena calidam potionem in pultario poposcit simulque personam eius diei acceptam intuens coronam e capite suo in eam transtulit, tali habitu rigens nullo sentiente, donec adcubantium proximus tepescere potionem admoneret.
pairs.question: Quo die M. Ofilius Hilarus, comoediarum histrio, inter convivium nullo sentiente mortuus est?
pairs.question_en: On what day did M. Ofilius Hilarus, the comic actor, die at his own banquet without anyone noticing?
pairs.derivation: The actor Ofilius Hilarus (named at 7.184) died at his birthday dinner, upright and crowned, gazing at that day's mask. Anchored to the named actor; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Pliny's model of an untroubled death, and a vivid picture of Roman stage life.

pairs.source_text: invenitur in actis, Felice russei auriga elato, in rogum eius unum e faventibus iecisse se, frivolum dictu, ne hoc gloriae artificis daretur, adversis studiis copia odorum corruptum criminantibus.
pairs.question: Cuius factionis auriga Felix fuit, in cuius rogum unus e faventibus se iecit?
pairs.question_en: Of which racing faction was the charioteer Felix, onto whose pyre one of his supporters threw himself?
pairs.derivation: The charioteer Felix of the russata factio and the fan who threw himself on his pyre, recorded in the acta. Anchored to the named charioteer and the incident; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and squarely in Roman circus culture (the colour-factions).

pairs.source_text: Ipsum cremare apud Romanos non fuit veteris instituti: terra condebantur. at postquam longinquis bellis obrutos erui cognovere, tunc institutum.
pairs.question: Quo modo Romani antiquitus mortuos condebant, priusquam cremare instituerent?
pairs.question_en: How did the Romans of old dispose of their dead, before they took up cremation?
pairs.answer_en: They buried them in the earth.
pairs.derivation: Pliny's statement that cremation was not the old Roman practice: burial in the earth came first. Anchored to Roman custom; short answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a central fact about Roman funerary practice.

pairs.source_text: at postquam longinquis bellis obrutos erui cognovere, tunc institutum. et tamen multae familiae priscos servavere ritus, sicut in Cornelia nemo ante Sullam dictatorem traditur crematus, idque voluisse veritum talionem eruto C. Mari cadavere.
pairs.question: In gente Cornelia quis primus crematus esse traditur?
pairs.question_en: In the Cornelian gens, who is said to have been the first to be cremated?
pairs.derivation: The Cornelii kept to inhumation until Sulla, who chose cremation for fear of reprisal after Marius's body had been dug up. Anchored to the named gens and man; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman burial custom.

pairs.source_text: emere ac vendere Mercurius, vindemiare instituit Liber pater; idem diadema, regium insigne, et triumphum invenit.
pairs.question: Quis emere ac vendere primus instituisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, first instituted buying and selling?
pairs.derivation: The first entry in Pliny's catalogue of inventors: Mercury as author of trade. Anchored to the named god and the invention; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Mercury as god of commerce is core Roman religion.

pairs.source_text: vindemiare instituit Liber pater; idem diadema, regium insigne, et triumphum invenit.
pairs.question: Quis, praeter vindemiam, diadema regium insigne et triumphum invenisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, besides the grape-harvest, is said by Pliny to have invented the royal diadem and the triumph?
pairs.derivation: Liber pater as inventor of the vintage, the diadem, and the triumph. Anchored to the three named inventions; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Bacchus's triumphal procession from India is a Roman commonplace.

pairs.source_text: Ceres frumenta, cum antea glande vescerentur, eadem molere et conficere in Attica, ut alii, et in Sicilia, ob id dea iudicata.
pairs.question: Quo cibo homines ante frumenta a Cerere inventa vescebantur, ut Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: On what food did men live before Ceres discovered grain, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: The canonical before-and-after of civilization: acorns until Ceres gave grain. Anchored to Ceres and the invention of corn; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a commonplace of Latin literature.

pairs.source_text: Ceres frumenta, cum antea glande vescerentur, eadem molere et conficere in Attica, ut alii, et in Sicilia, ob id dea iudicata.
pairs.question: Cuius inventum frumenta fuisse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whose discovery does Pliny say grain was?
pairs.derivation: Ceres as discoverer of grain and of milling and baking, for which she was judged a goddess. Anchored to the invention; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Ceres and corn is foundational Roman religion.

pairs.source_text: utrique in Graeciam attulisse e Phoenice Cadmum sedecim numero, quibus Troiano bello Palameden adiecisse quattuor hac figura ΖΨΞΧ, totidem post eum Simoniden melicum ΨΞΩΘ.
pairs.question: Quot litteras Palamedes Troiano bello adiecisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: How many letters is Palamedes said to have added at the time of the Trojan war?
pairs.derivation: In Pliny's history of the alphabet, Palamedes added four letters to Cadmus's sixteen (Simonides four more). Anchored to Palamedes and the Trojan war; single number answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and part of the standard ancient account of the alphabet.

pairs.source_text: ex quo apparet aeternus litterarum usus. in Latium eas attulerunt Pelasgi.
pairs.question: Qui litteras in Latium attulisse a Plinio traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, brought letters into Latium?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's statement that the Pelasgi carried the alphabet to Latium. Anchored to Latium; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the counterpart, for Rome, of Cadmus bringing letters to Greece.

pairs.source_text: oppidum Cecrops a se appellavit Cecropiam, quae nunc est arx Athenis.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Cecrops oppidum a se conditum appellavit, quod nunc arx Athenarum est?
pairs.question_en: By what name did Cecrops call the town he founded, which is now the citadel of Athens?
pairs.derivation: Cecrops named his foundation Cecropia, later the Acropolis of Athens. Anchored to Cecrops and Athens; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cecrops as founder of Athens is standard Greek legend.

pairs.source_text: tegulas invenit Cinyra, Agriopae filius, et metalla aeris, utrumque in insula Cypro, item forcipem, martulum, vectem, incudem.
pairs.question: In qua insula Cinyra, Agriopae filius, tegulas et aeris metalla invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: On which island is Cinyras, son of Agriopa, said to have invented roof-tiles and copper mines?
pairs.derivation: Cinyras of Cyprus as inventor of tiles and of copper-mining, both on his island. Anchored to the named man; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cyprus is the ancient world's byword for copper (cuprum).

pairs.source_text: puteos Danaus ex Aegypto advectus in Graeciam qua vocabatur Argos Dipsion; lapidicinas Cadmus Thebis turres, ut Aristoteles, Cyclopes, Tirynthii, ut Theophrastus.
pairs.question: Quis puteos ex Aegypto in Graeciam attulisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have brought wells from Egypt into Greece?
pairs.derivation: Danaus brought well-digging from Egypt to the thirsty Argive plain (Argos Dipsion). Anchored to Danaus, Egypt, and Argos; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book Greek foundation legend.

pairs.source_text: lapidicinas Cadmus Thebis turres, ut Aristoteles, Cyclopes, Tirynthii, ut Theophrastus.
pairs.question: Quos turrium inventores Aristoteles fecisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Aristotle, as reported by Pliny, make the inventors of towers?
pairs.derivation: Aristotle credited towers to the Cyclopes (Theophrastus to the Tirynthians). Anchored to Aristotle's attribution; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: 'Cyclopean' walls are ambient ancient knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Aegyptii textilia, inficere lanas Sardibus Lydi, fusos in lanificio Closter, filius Arachnae, linum et retia Arachne, fulloniam artem Nicias Megarensis, sutrinam Tychius Boeotius.
pairs.question: Qui lanas inficere Sardibus primi instituisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have been the first to dye wool, at Sardis?
pairs.derivation: The Lydians of Sardis as inventors of wool-dyeing. Anchored to Sardis; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Lydian purple and dyed wool are a fixture of ancient luxury lore.

pairs.source_text: linum et retia Arachne, fulloniam artem Nicias Megarensis, sutrinam Tychius Boeotius.
pairs.question: Quae linum et retia invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented linen thread and nets?
pairs.derivation: Arachne credited with flax-thread and nets (her son Closter with spindles). Anchored to the named figure; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Arachne the weaver is canonical myth.

pairs.source_text: medicinam Aegyptii apud ipsos volunt repertam, alii per Arabum, Babylonis et Apollinis filium, herbariam et medicamentariam a Chirone, Saturni et Philyrae filio.
pairs.question: Cui, Saturni et Philyrae filio, herbaria et medicamentaria ars inventa tribuitur?
pairs.question_en: To whom, the son of Saturn and Philyra, is the discovery of herbal and drug medicine attributed?
pairs.derivation: Chiron the centaur as founder of herbal medicine. Anchored by the named parentage; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Chiron the healer and teacher of Asclepius and Achilles is standard myth.

pairs.source_text: ferrum Hesiodus in Creta eo qui vocati sunt Dactyli Idaei.
pairs.question: Quibus Hesiodus ferri inventionem in Creta tribuit?
pairs.question_en: To whom does Hesiod attribute the discovery of iron in Crete?
pairs.derivation: Hesiod's attribution of iron-working to the Idaean Dactyls of Crete. Anchored to Hesiod and Crete; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Dactyls are the standard mythic smiths.

pairs.source_text: plumbum ex Cassiteride insula primus adportavit Midacritus.
pairs.question: Ex qua insula Midacritus plumbum primus adportavit?
pairs.question_en: From which island did Midacritus first bring lead (tin)?
pairs.derivation: The first importation of tin/lead from the Cassiterides (the 'Tin Islands'). Anchored to the named man and island; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Cassiterides are the famous tin-source of ancient geography.

pairs.source_text: fabricam ferrariam invenerunt Cyclopes, figlinas Coroebus Atheniensis, in iis orbem Anarcharsis Scythes, ut alii, Hyperbius Corinthius.
pairs.question: Quis figlinas invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented potteries?
pairs.derivation: Coroebus of Athens as inventor of the potter's craft (the wheel being credited to Anacharsis or Hyperbius). Anchored to the craft; single named answer supported verbatim, with no rival attribution for the craft itself. Closed-book entry of Pliny's inventor-catalogue.

pairs.source_text: fabricam materiariam Daedalus et in ea serram, asciam, perpendiculum, terebram, glutinum, ichthyocollam.
pairs.question: Cui fabrica materiaria et in ea serra, ascia, perpendiculum, terebra inventa tribuuntur?
pairs.question_en: To whom are carpentry, and in it the saw, adze, plumb-line, and drill, attributed as inventions?
pairs.derivation: Daedalus as inventor of carpentry and its tools. Anchored to the named craft and tools; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Daedalus the archetypal craftsman.

pairs.source_text: normam autem et libellam et tornum et clavem Theodorus Samius, mensuras et pondera Phidon Argivus aut Palamedes, ut maluit Gellius.
pairs.question: Quis normam et libellam et tornum et clavem invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the square, the level, the lathe, and the key?
pairs.derivation: Theodorus of Samos credited with the carpenter's square, level, lathe, and key. Anchored to the named tools; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Theodorus is one of the best-known archaic Greek craftsmen.

pairs.source_text: ignem e silice Pyrodes Cilicis filius, eundem adservare ferula Prometheus.
pairs.question: Quis ignem ferula adservare docuisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have taught men to keep fire in a fennel-stalk?
pairs.derivation: Prometheus preserved fire in the ferula (narthex), while Pyrodes struck it from flint. Anchored to the named act; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the fennel-stalk is the canonical detail of the Prometheus myth.

pairs.source_text: vehiculum cum quattuor rotis Phryges, mercaturas Poeni, culturas vitium et arborum Eumolpus Atheniensis, vinum aquae misceri Staphylus Silieni filius, oleum et trapetas Aristaeus Atheniensis, idem mella.
pairs.question: Qui vehiculum cum quattuor rotis invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented the four-wheeled vehicle?
pairs.derivation: The Phrygians credited with the four-wheeled wagon (as with the biga). Anchored to the named invention; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of the inventor-catalogue.

pairs.source_text: vehiculum cum quattuor rotis Phryges, mercaturas Poeni, culturas vitium et arborum Eumolpus Atheniensis.
pairs.question: Qui mercaturas invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented commerce?
pairs.derivation: Trade credited to the Poeni. Anchored to the named invention; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Carthaginian/Phoenician trader is one of the ancient world's fixed cultural images.

pairs.source_text: vinum aquae misceri Staphylus Silieni filius, oleum et trapetas Aristaeus Atheniensis, idem mella.
pairs.question: Quis vinum aqua misceri primus instituisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have first instituted the mixing of wine with water?
pairs.derivation: Staphylus as inventor of diluting wine with water — the normal ancient way of drinking. Anchored to the named figure and practice; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and central to Greco-Roman drinking custom.

pairs.source_text: oleum et trapetas Aristaeus Atheniensis, idem mella.
pairs.question: Cui oleum et trapetae, idem et mella, inventa tribuuntur?
pairs.question_en: To whom are olive oil and the olive-press, and honey too, attributed as discoveries?
pairs.derivation: Aristaeus credited with oil, the trapetum, and honey. Anchored to the named products; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Aristaeus is the mythic patron of bee-keeping and the olive (cf. Vergil, Georgics 4).

pairs.source_text: culturas vitium et arborum Eumolpus Atheniensis, vinum aquae misceri Staphylus Silieni filius.
pairs.question: Quis culturas vitium et arborum invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the cultivation of vines and trees?
pairs.derivation: Eumolpus of Athens credited with viticulture and arboriculture. Anchored to the named arts; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of Pliny's catalogue, and Eumolpus is a familiar Eleusinian name.

pairs.source_text: regiam civitatem Aegyptii, popularem Attici post Theseum. tyrannus primus fuit Phalaris Agraganti. servitium invenere Lacedaemonii. iudicium capitis in Areopago primum actum est.
pairs.question: Post quem Attici popularem civitatem habuisse a Plinio traduntur?
pairs.question_en: After whom, according to Pliny, did the Athenians have a popular (democratic) government?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's constitutional firsts: monarchy from the Egyptians, democracy at Athens after Theseus. Anchored to the Attici and the constitution; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Theseus as the founder of the Athenian polity is standard.

pairs.source_text: servitium invenere Lacedaemonii. iudicium capitis in Areopago primum actum est.
pairs.question: Qui servitium invenisse a Plinio traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented slavery?
pairs.derivation: Pliny credits the invention of slavery to the Lacedaemonians (the helot system). Anchored to the named people; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, and a pointed item of ancient social history.

pairs.source_text: iudicium capitis in Areopago primum actum est.
pairs.question: Ubi iudicium capitis primum actum esse Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Where does Pliny say the first capital trial was held?
pairs.derivation: The Areopagus as the site of the first trial for a capital charge. Anchored to the named court; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Areopagus is the archetypal homicide court of the ancient world.

pairs.source_text: clupeos invenerunt Proetus et Acrisius inter se bellantes sive Chalcus Athamantis filius, loricam Midias Messenius, galeam, gladium, hastam Lacedaemonii, ocreas et cristas Cares.
pairs.question: Qui galeam, gladium, hastam invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented the helmet, the sword, and the spear?
pairs.derivation: Pliny's attribution of helmet, sword, and spear to the Lacedaemonians. Anchored to the named arms; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, and consistent with Sparta's ambient reputation in arms.

pairs.source_text: loricam Midias Messenius, galeam, gladium, hastam Lacedaemonii, ocreas et cristas Cares.
pairs.question: Qui ocreas et cristas invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented greaves and helmet-crests?
pairs.derivation: Greaves and crests credited to the Carians. Anchored to the named items; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Herodotus too makes the Carians the inventors of crests and shield-devices.

pairs.source_text: lanceas Aetolos, iaculum cum ammento Aetolum Martis filium, hastas velitares Tyrrenum, eundem pilum, Penthesileam Amazonem securim, Pisaeum venabula et in tormentis scorpionem, Cretas catapultam, Syrophoenicas ballistam et fundam.
pairs.question: Cui Amazoni securis inventio tribuitur?
pairs.question_en: To which Amazon is the invention of the battle-axe attributed?
pairs.derivation: The battle-axe credited to the Amazon Penthesilea. Anchored to the named figure and weapon; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Penthesilea and the Amazons' axe are canonical.

pairs.source_text: Cretas catapultam, Syrophoenicas ballistam et fundam, aeneam tubam Pisaeum Tyrreni, testudines Artemonem Clazomenium.
pairs.question: Qui catapultam invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented the catapult?
pairs.derivation: The catapult credited to the Cretans (the ballista and sling to the Syrophoenicians). Anchored to the named engine; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of the catalogue of military inventions.

pairs.source_text: equum (qui nunc aries appellatur) in muralibus machinis Epium ad Troiam, equo vehi Bellerophontem, frenos et strata equorum Pelethronium, pugnare ex equo Thessalos, qui Centauri appellati sunt, habitantes secundum Pelium montem.
pairs.question: Quis equum illum, qui nunc aries appellatur, in muralibus machinis ad Troiam invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have devised at Troy the 'horse' among siege-engines, now called the ram?
pairs.derivation: Epeus, maker of the Trojan Horse, credited with the siege-engine now called the ram. Anchored to Troy and the engine; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Epeus and the wooden horse are canonical.

pairs.source_text: equo vehi Bellerophontem, frenos et strata equorum Pelethronium, pugnare ex equo Thessalos, qui Centauri appellati sunt, habitantes secundum Pelium montem.
pairs.question: Quis primus equo vehi coepisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have been the first to ride on horseback?
pairs.derivation: Bellerophon as the first rider. Anchored to the named hero; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Bellerophon and Pegasus are canonical myth.

pairs.source_text: pugnare ex equo Thessalos, qui Centauri appellati sunt, habitantes secundum Pelium montem.
pairs.question: Qui primi ex equo pugnare instituisse traduntur, qui Centauri appellati sunt?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have first fought on horseback, and were called Centaurs?
pairs.derivation: The rationalizing explanation of the Centaurs as the Thessalian horsemen of Pelion. Anchored to the Centaurs and Mount Pelion; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a well-known ancient rationalization.

pairs.source_text: bigas prima iunxit Phrygum natio, quadrigas Erichthonius.
pairs.question: Quae natio bigas prima iunxisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Which nation, according to Pliny, first yoked the two-horse chariot?
pairs.derivation: The biga credited to the Phrygians (the quadriga to Erichthonius). Anchored to the named vehicle; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of the catalogue; distinct from the quadriga fact already taken.

pairs.source_text: ordinem exercitus, signi dationem, tesseras, vigilias Palamedes invenit Troiano bello, specularum significationem eodem Sinon, inducias Lycaon, foedera Theseus.
pairs.question: Quis ordinem exercitus, signi dationem, tesseras et vigilias Troiano bello invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented, in the Trojan war, the ordering of an army, the giving of the signal, watchwords, and sentry-duty?
pairs.derivation: Palamedes as the inventor of military organization. Anchored to the Trojan war and the named institutions; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Palamedes the culture-hero of the Greek camp.

pairs.source_text: specularum significationem eodem Sinon, inducias Lycaon, foedera Theseus.
pairs.question: Quis foedera invenisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented treaties?
pairs.derivation: Treaties credited to Theseus (truces to Lycaon). Anchored to the named institution; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of the catalogue, tied to Athens's founding hero.

pairs.source_text: Auguria ex avibus Car, a quo Caria appellata; adiecit ex ceteris animalibus Orpheus, aruspicia Delphus, ignispicia Amphiaraus, extispicia avium Tiresias Thebanus, interpretationem ostentorum et somniorum Amphictyon.
pairs.question: A quo auguria ex avibus inventa esse traduntur, a quo etiam Caria appellata est?
pairs.question_en: By whom are bird-auguries said to have been invented, the man from whom Caria took its name?
pairs.derivation: Car, eponym of Caria, as inventor of augury from birds. Anchored by the eponymy; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: augury from birds is the central Roman divinatory art, and Pliny's catalogue of its origins is standard learning.

pairs.source_text: aruspicia Delphus, ignispicia Amphiaraus, extispicia avium Tiresias Thebanus, interpretationem ostentorum et somniorum Amphictyon.
pairs.question: Quis ignispicia invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented divination by fire?
pairs.derivation: Amphiaraus credited with ignispicium, divination from fire. Anchored to the named art; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Amphiaraus is the archetypal seer of the Theban cycle.

pairs.source_text: aruspicia Delphus, ignispicia Amphiaraus, extispicia avium Tiresias Thebanus, interpretationem ostentorum et somniorum Amphictyon.
pairs.question: Quis extispicia avium invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented divination from the entrails of birds?
pairs.derivation: Tiresias credited with inspection of birds' entrails. Anchored to the named seer and art; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Tiresias is the best-known seer of Greek myth.

pairs.source_text: interpretationem ostentorum et somniorum Amphictyon. astrologiam Atlans Libyae filius, ut alii, Aegyptii, ut alii, Assyrii, sphaeram in ea Milesius Anaximander, ventorum rationem Aeolus Hellenis filius.
pairs.question: Quis interpretationem ostentorum et somniorum invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the interpretation of portents and dreams?
pairs.derivation: Amphictyon credited with the reading of portents and dreams. Anchored to the named art; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of Pliny's catalogue of divinatory origins.

pairs.source_text: astrologiam Atlans Libyae filius, ut alii, Aegyptii, ut alii, Assyrii, sphaeram in ea Milesius Anaximander, ventorum rationem Aeolus Hellenis filius.
pairs.question: Quis sphaeram invenisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented the celestial globe?
pairs.derivation: Anaximander credited with the sphaera within astronomy. Anchored to the named instrument; single named answer supported verbatim (no rival attribution for the sphere itself). Closed-book fact of the history of science.

pairs.source_text: sphaeram in ea Milesius Anaximander, ventorum rationem Aeolus Hellenis filius.
pairs.question: Cui, Hellenis filio, ventorum ratio inventa tribuitur?
pairs.question_en: To whom, the son of Hellen, is the science of the winds attributed?
pairs.derivation: Aeolus son of Hellen credited with the theory of the winds. Anchored by the named parentage; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Aeolus as lord of the winds is canonical (Odyssey 10, Aeneid 1).

pairs.source_text: musicam Amphion, fistulam et monaulum Pan Mercuri, obliquam tibiam Midas in Phrygia, geminas tibias Marsyas in eadem gente.
pairs.question: Quis fistulam et monaulum invenisse traditur, Mercuri filius?
pairs.question_en: Who, the son of Mercury, is said to have invented the pan-pipe and the single flute?
pairs.derivation: Pan credited with the syrinx and monaulos. Anchored by the named parentage and instrument; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the pan-pipe is one of the most recognizable attributes in ancient culture.

pairs.source_text: obliquam tibiam Midas in Phrygia, geminas tibias Marsyas in eadem gente.
pairs.question: Quis geminas tibias in Phrygia invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the double pipes in Phrygia?
pairs.derivation: Marsyas the Phrygian credited with the double aulos (and with the Phrygian modes). Anchored to Phrygia and the instrument; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Marsyas and his pipes, and his contest with Apollo, are canonical.

pairs.source_text: septem chordis primum cecinit III ad IIII primas additis Terpander, octavam Simonides addidit, nonam Timotheus.
pairs.question: Quis primus septem chordis cecinisse traditur, tribus ad quattuor primas additis?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have been the first to sing to seven strings, adding three to the original four?
pairs.derivation: Terpander's seven-stringed lyre, the foundational fact of Greek music history (Simonides added the eighth string, Timotheus the ninth). Anchored to the named musician and number; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

pairs.source_text: septem chordis primum cecinit III ad IIII primas additis Terpander, octavam Simonides addidit, nonam Timotheus.
pairs.question: Quis nonam chordam citharae addidisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have added the ninth string to the lyre?
pairs.derivation: Timotheus of Miletus added the ninth string, the notorious musical innovation of the late fifth century. Anchored to the numbered string; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Greek music.

pairs.source_text: saltationem armatam Curetes docuere, pyrrichen Pyrrus, utramque in Creta.
pairs.question: Qui saltationem armatam in Creta docuisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have taught the armed dance in Crete?
pairs.derivation: The Curetes as teachers of the armed dance in Crete (the pyrrhic being credited to Pyrrhus). Anchored to Crete and the dance; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Curetes' clashing armour around the infant Jupiter is standard myth.

pairs.source_text: saltationem armatam Curetes docuere, pyrrichen Pyrrus, utramque in Creta.
pairs.question: A quo pyrriche saltatio inventa esse traditur?
pairs.question_en: By whom is the pyrrhic dance said to have been invented?
pairs.derivation: The pyrriche credited to Pyrrhus, in Crete. Anchored to the named dance; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the pyrrhic war-dance was still performed in Roman spectacle.

pairs.source_text: versum heroum Pythio oraculo debemus.
pairs.question: Cui rei versum heroum deberi Plinius scribit?
pairs.question_en: To what does Pliny say we owe the heroic verse (hexameter)?
pairs.derivation: Pliny derives the hexameter from Delphi. Anchored to the metre and the oracle; single answer supported verbatim. The fact translates (the origin of a verse-form), so it stays on the main track. Closed-book learned tradition.

pairs.source_text: prosam orationem condere Pherecydes Syrius instituit Cyri regis aetate, historiam Cadmus Milesius.
pairs.question: Quis prosam orationem condere primus instituisse traditur, Cyri regis aetate?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have been the first to compose in prose, in the age of king Cyrus?
pairs.derivation: Pherecydes of Syros as the first prose writer. Anchored to the age of Cyrus; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book landmark in the history of Greek literature.

pairs.source_text: prosam orationem condere Pherecydes Syrius instituit Cyri regis aetate, historiam Cadmus Milesius.
pairs.question: Quis historiam scribere primus instituisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, first wrote history?
pairs.derivation: Cadmus of Miletus as the first historian. Anchored to the genre; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of literary history, distinct from the Cadmus of the alphabet.

pairs.source_text: ludos gymnicos in Arcadia Lycaon, funebres Acastus in Iolco, post eum Theseus in Isthmo, Hercules Olympiae; athleticam Pittheus, pilam lusoriam Gyges Lydus.
pairs.question: Quis ludos Olympiae instituisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, founded the games at Olympia?
pairs.derivation: Hercules as founder of the Olympic games in Pliny's series of games-founders. Anchored to Olympia; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the standard ancient account of the Olympics' origin.

pairs.source_text: ludos gymnicos in Arcadia Lycaon, funebres Acastus in Iolco, post eum Theseus in Isthmo, Hercules Olympiae.
pairs.question: Quis ludos funebres in Iolco primus fecisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have first held funeral games, at Iolcos?
pairs.derivation: Acastus's funeral games at Iolcos (for Pelias), the first of their kind, before Theseus at the Isthmus. Anchored to Iolcos; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: funeral games are a defining institution of the heroic age.

pairs.source_text: athleticam Pittheus, pilam lusoriam Gyges Lydus; picturam Aegyptii et in Graecia Euchir, Daedali cognatus, ut Aristoteli placet, ut Theophrasto, Polygnotus Atheniensis.
pairs.question: Quis pilam lusoriam invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the game of ball?
pairs.derivation: Ball-play credited to Gyges the Lydian. Anchored to the named game; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: ball games were an everyday Roman leisure activity, and this is their canonical origin-story.

pairs.source_text: Nave primus in Graeciam ex Aegypto Danaus advenit; antea ratibus navigabatur inventis in mari Rubro inter insulas a rege Erythra.
pairs.question: Quis primus nave ex Aegypto in Graeciam advenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have been the first to come by ship from Egypt to Greece?
pairs.derivation: Danaus's voyage as the first use of a ship into Greece. Anchored to Egypt and Greece; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Danaus and his daughters are canonical Greek legend.

pairs.source_text: antea ratibus navigabatur inventis in mari Rubro inter insulas a rege Erythra.
pairs.question: A quo rege rates in mari Rubro inventae esse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: By which king are rafts said to have been invented, among the islands of the Red Sea?
pairs.derivation: King Erythras, eponym of the Erythraean (Red) Sea, credited with the raft. Anchored to the named sea and king; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book piece of ancient geography-lore.

pairs.source_text: longe nave Iasonem primum navigasse Philostephanus auctor est, Hegesias Parhalum, Ctesias Samiramin, Archemachus Aegaeonem, biremem Damastes Erythraeos fecisse, triremem Thucydides Aminoclen Corinthium.
pairs.question: Quem primum longa nave navigasse Philostephanus auctor est?
pairs.question_en: Who, on the authority of Philostephanus, was the first to sail in a long ship?
pairs.derivation: Jason and the Argo as the first long ship, on Philostephanus's authority (Pliny lists rival claims under other authors, so the attribution is anchored to its source). Anchored to Jason and the named authority; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: the Argo is the archetypal first ship.

pairs.source_text: biremem Damastes Erythraeos fecisse, triremem Thucydides Aminoclen Corinthium, quadriremem Aristoteles Carthaginienses.
pairs.question: Quem triremis inventorem Thucydides facit?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Thucydides make the inventor of the trireme?
pairs.derivation: Thucydides' attribution of the trireme to Ameinocles of Corinth (Thuc. 1.13). Anchored to Thucydides and the ship-type; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of naval history.

pairs.source_text: triremem Thucydides Aminoclen Corinthium, quadriremem Aristoteles Carthaginienses.
pairs.question: Quos quadriremis inventores Aristoteles facit?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Aristotle make the inventors of the quadrireme?
pairs.derivation: Aristotle's attribution of the four-banked ship to Carthage. Anchored to Aristotle and the ship-type; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of naval history.

pairs.source_text: ad quindecim Demetrium Antigoni, ad XXX Ptolemaeum Philadelphum, ad XL Ptolemaeum Philopatorem, qui Tryphon cognominatus est.
pairs.question: Quis rex navem usque ad quadraginta ordines auxisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Which king is said to have built up a ship to as many as forty banks of oars?
pairs.derivation: The escalating scale of Hellenistic warships culminates in Ptolemy Philopator's forty-banked ship. Anchored to the named king and number; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Hellenistic naval extravagance.

pairs.source_text: siderum observationem in navigando Phoenices, remum Copae, latitudinem eius Plataeae, vela Icarus, malum et antennam Daedalus.
pairs.question: Qui siderum observationem in navigando invenisse traduntur?
pairs.question_en: Who are said to have invented observation of the stars in navigation?
pairs.derivation: Star-navigation credited to the Phoenicians. Anchored to the named art; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Phoenician seamanship is one of antiquity's fixed cultural facts.

pairs.source_text: vela Icarus, malum et antennam Daedalus, hippegum Samii aut Pericles Atheniensis, tectas longas Thasii.
pairs.question: Quis vela invenisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented sails?
pairs.derivation: Sails credited to Icarus, mast and yard to Daedalus — the rationalized version of the flight-myth. Anchored to the named invention; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and tied to one of the most familiar myths.

pairs.source_text: vela Icarus, malum et antennam Daedalus, hippegum Samii aut Pericles Atheniensis.
pairs.question: Quis malum et antennam invenisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, invented the mast and the yard-arm?
pairs.derivation: Mast and yard credited to Daedalus, beside Icarus's sails. Anchored to the named parts of a ship; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book entry of the catalogue.

pairs.source_text: rostra addidit Pisaeus Tyrreni, ancoram Eupalamus, eandem bidentem Anacharsis, harpagones et manus Pericles Atheniensis, adminicula gubernandi Tiphys.
pairs.question: Quis ancoram bidentem invenisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who is said to have invented the two-fluked anchor?
pairs.derivation: The double-fluked anchor credited to Anacharsis the Scythian (the plain anchor to Eupalamus). Anchored to the named object; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: Anacharsis is a famous ancient culture-hero of invention.

pairs.source_text: harpagones et manus Pericles Atheniensis, adminicula gubernandi Tiphys. classe princeps depugnavit Minos.
pairs.question: Quis princeps classe depugnavisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, was the first to fight a battle with a fleet?
pairs.derivation: Minos as the first to fight a naval battle, matching the tradition of the Cretan thalassocracy. Anchored to the named king; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and a standard ancient claim (cf. Thucydides 1.4).

pairs.source_text: Animal occidit primus Hyperbius Martis filius, Prometheus bovem.
pairs.question: Quis primus bovem occidisse a Plinio traditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to Pliny, was the first to kill an ox?
pairs.derivation: Prometheus as the first to slaughter an ox (Hyperbius the first to kill any animal) — the origin of blood sacrifice and meat-eating. Anchored to the named act; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and tied to the Promethean sacrifice-myth.

pairs.source_text: Sequens gentium consensus in tonsoribus fuit, sed Romanis tardior. in Italiam ex Sicilia venere post Romam conditam anno CCCCLIIII adducente P. Titinio Mena, ut auctor est Varro; antea intonsi fuere.
pairs.question: Ex qua insula tonsores in Italiam venisse Varro auctor est?
pairs.question_en: From which island does Varro record that barbers came into Italy?
pairs.derivation: Barbers reached Italy from Sicily, on Varro's authority; before that the Romans went unshorn. Anchored to Varro and Italy; single place answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman daily life.

pairs.source_text: in Italiam ex Sicilia venere post Romam conditam anno CCCCLIIII adducente P. Titinio Mena, ut auctor est Varro; antea intonsi fuere.
pairs.question: A quo tonsores in Italiam adducti esse dicuntur, ut Varro tradit?
pairs.question_en: By whom are barbers said to have been brought into Italy, according to Varro?
pairs.derivation: P. Titinius Mena brought the first barbers to Italy in the 454th year of the city. Anchored to Varro and the date; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact about Roman grooming custom.

pairs.source_text: primus omnium radi cotidie instituit Africanus sequens; Divus Augustus cultris semper usus est.
pairs.question: Quis primus omnium cotidie radi instituit, ut Plinius tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first of all to be shaved daily, according to Pliny?
pairs.derivation: Scipio Aemilianus as the first Roman to shave every day. Anchored to the named man; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book detail of Roman grooming and self-presentation.

pairs.source_text: primus omnium radi cotidie instituit Africanus sequens; Divus Augustus cultris semper usus est.
pairs.question: Quo instrumento Divus Augustus in tondendo semper usus est?
pairs.question_en: What implement did the deified Augustus always use for his grooming?
pairs.derivation: Augustus always used cultri rather than the razor. Anchored to Augustus; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book detail of the emperor's personal habits, in Pliny's section on the consensus about barbers.

pairs.source_text: XII tabulis ortus tantum et occasus nominantur, post aliquot annos adiectus est et meridies, accenso consulum id pronuntiante, cum a curia inter Rostra et Graecostasin prospexisset solem.
pairs.question: Quae duo tantum diei tempora in XII tabulis nominantur?
pairs.question_en: Which two times of day alone are named in the Twelve Tables?
pairs.derivation: The Twelve Tables recognized only sunrise and sunset; midday was added later. Anchored to the Twelve Tables; the two-part answer is a fixed pair quoted verbatim. Closed-book fact about Rome's oldest law code and its reckoning of time.

pairs.source_text: post aliquot annos adiectus est et meridies, accenso consulum id pronuntiante, cum a curia inter Rostra et Graecostasin prospexisset solem; a columna Maenia ad carcerem inclinato sidere supremam pronuntiavit, sed hoc serenis tantum diebus, usque ad primum Punicum bellum.
pairs.question: Quis Romae meridiem pronuntiabat, cum a curia inter Rostra et Graecostasin solem prospexisset?
pairs.question_en: Who at Rome announced midday, after looking out for the sun from the senate-house between the Rostra and the Graecostasis?
pairs.derivation: The consuls' accensus proclaimed midday, and the last hour when the sun sank between the Maenian column and the prison. Anchored to the Roman forum and the office; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book detail of how Romans told the time.

pairs.source_text: princeps solarium horologium statuisse ante XII annos quam cum Pyrro bellatum est ad aedem Quirini L. Papirius Cursor, cum eam dedicaret a patre suo votam, a Fabio Vestale proditur.
pairs.question: Quis primus solarium horologium ad aedem Quirini statuisse a Fabio Vestale proditur?
pairs.question_en: Who, on the authority of Fabius Vestalis, was the first to set up a sundial, at the temple of Quirinus?
pairs.derivation: The first sundial at Rome, set up by Papirius Cursor at the temple of Quirinus twelve years before the war with Pyrrhus. Anchored to the named man, temple, and authority; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman time-keeping.

pairs.source_text: M. Varro primum statutum in publico secundum Rostra in columna tradit bello Punico primo a M'. Valerio Messala cos. Catina capta in Sicilia, deportatum inde post XXX annos quam de Papiriano horologio traditur, anno urbis CCCCLXXXX.
pairs.question: Unde M'. Valerius Messala consul horologium illud deportavit, quod primum in publico secundum Rostra statutum est?
pairs.question_en: From where did the consul M'. Valerius Messala bring the sundial that was the first set up in a public place beside the Rostra?
pairs.derivation: The first public sundial at Rome was war-booty from the capture of Catina in the First Punic War, on Varro's authority. Anchored to the named consul and city; single answer supported verbatim. Closed-book fact of Roman public life.

pairs.source_text: tunc Scipio Nasica collega Laenati primus aqua divisit horas aeque noctium ac dierum idque horologium sub tecto dicavit anno urbis DXCV. tam diu populo Romano indiscreta lux fuit.
pairs.question: Quis primus Romae aqua horas et noctium et dierum divisit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first at Rome to measure the hours of night as well as of day by water?
pairs.derivation: Scipio Nasica, colleague of Laenas, dedicated Rome's first water-clock under cover in the 595th year of the city. Anchored to the named censor and the clepsydra; single named answer supported verbatim. Closed-book landmark of Roman time-keeping.
